docs.title: Postal
docs.text:
A modern email library for CodeIgniter 4.

Write a message once and send it through SMTP, Amazon SES, Resend, sendmail or a failover chain. You choose the provider in config, not code. Existing service('email') calls keep working, so you can adopt Postal one step at a time.

composer require myth/postal

Requires PHP 8.2+ and CodeIgniter 4.7+. See Installation for extensions and configuration.

docs.title: See it in action
Why Postal
docs.text:
• Deliver anywhere

    SMTP, sendmail, Amazon SES and Resend, with failover between them and DKIM signing. Or write your own transport.

  • Write mail as classes

    Mailables keep each email in one class, written in HTML or Markdown with a shared layout, and previewed in the browser.

  • Send safely

    A suppression list filters recipients and List-Unsubscribe headers are added for you. Events let you change or stop any send.

  • Test without sending

    Mailer::fake() records every message so your tests can assert on it, with no network access.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Markdown: the plain-text part broke URLs that held a pair of _, *, **, ~~ or backticks, such as https://example.com/_promo_/x. The emphasis rules stripped the pair, so the link went somewhere else. MarkdownRenderer::toText() now leaves link targets, Mail Component url values and bare http(s) URLs unchanged (#56).
  • Legacy adapter: Shield's emailer() threw a TypeError. LegacyEmailAdapter now extends CodeIgniter\Email\Email, so Shield's emails send through Postal. Subclasses that override a method with typed parameters must drop the types. initialize() now clears the message first, as the framework's does. See ADR 0002 (#52).
  • Markdown: the plain-text part of a markdown() Mailable kept Mail Component tags, so text-only readers saw raw <mail-button url="..."> markup and the button's URL was hidden in an attribute. MarkdownRenderer::toText() now replaces each component with its slot text, followed by its url in parentheses when it has one, like a markdown link (#50).
  • Preview: every link on the preview index failed. The class went into the URL as App%5CMails%5CWelcomeEmail, and CodeIgniter rejects the decoded backslashes because they aren't in the default App::$permittedURIChars. The links now write the class with dots (App.Mails.WelcomeEmail), which the preview maps back to the class name (#48).
  • Mail Components: <mail-button> emitted its url through the attr escaper context, which is meant for unquoted attribute values and encodes every non-alphanumeric character. The href came out as https://example.com — which email clients still follow, but which hides the link from anything post-processing the rendered HTML by matching href="http...", such as click tracking or link rewriting. The href is double-quoted, so the html context is the correct one: it neutralises the characters that could end the attribute and leaves the URL readable.
  • Mail Components: <mail-panel>'s color never reached the email. It was emitted through the css escaper, which encodes # as \23, producing background-color: \23 eff6ff — an ident token where a hash token is required, so the declaration was invalid and dropped. Panels rendered with no background at all, including at the default colour. The value is now validated as a hex colour or colour keyword, falling back to the default when it is neither: for a value that lands in a CSS property position, escaping and rendering are mutually exclusive, so validation is the only workable approach.
  • Mail Components: each component now renders with saveData off. CodeIgniter's renderer carries view data between render() calls, so an optional attribute set on one component leaked into the next component that omitted it — a <mail-panel> with no color picked up the colour of an earlier panel in the same email.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Legacy adapter (behaviour change): once an app publishes its own Config\Mailer, the legacy adapter sends through the default mailer (service('mailer')->mailer()) instead of building a transport from Config\Email. The flat transport keys (protocol, mailPath, SMTP*, DSN) are ignored, including those passed to initialize() or setProtocol(), so Shield's emailer() and other service('email') code now use the configured mailer. Message keys (mailType, wordWrap, priority, BCCBatch*, …) work as before. Apps without a published Config\Mailer are unaffected (#61).
  • Legacy adapter: protocol is now case-insensitive. CodeIgniter's own setProtocol() checks the value before lowercasing it, so 'SMTP' silently sent through mail(). The adapter and LegacyConfigMapper now send 'SMTP' through SMTP. If an app's protocol is mixed-case, check its SMTP settings before upgrading (#60).
  • Mailable::render() now sets Email::$mailableClass (before, only send() did), and the Events docs describe it. It holds the class name of the Mailable that built the message, so email.composing, email.sending, email.sent and email.failed listeners can tell which Mailable produced a send. Messages built with new Email() or through the legacy adapter carry null. The value is never written into the MIME message (#51).
  • BREAKING: the mailer configuration class is now Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer (was Myth\Postal\Config\Email), and MailerManager resolves it by its short name. The old name collided with the framework's legacy Config\Email, which forced resolution by fully-qualified class name — and that form never consults an application subclass, so the documented override path could not work. Applications that published a Config\Email extending the package config should rename it to Config\Mailer and extend Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer. The framework's own legacy Config\Email, used by LegacyEmailAdapter and spark email:test, is unaffected. See ADR 0001.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Myth\Postal\LegacyConfigMapper::toMailer(): turns CodeIgniter's flat Config\Email keys into a Postal mailer definition, using the same rules as LegacyEmailAdapter. Other packages can move legacy settings into Config\Mailer without changing how mail is sent. The adapter now builds its transport through it (#60).
  • Myth\Postal\Preview\MailablePreviewer: the discovery and rendering behind the browser preview, as a public class, so a host application can build its own preview screens. It takes a namespace => directory map, finds the previewable Mailables in it (discover()), checks an untrusted class name (isPreviewable()), returns just a class's subject for list screens (subject()), and renders one class to a MailablePreview holding the subject, HTML, text (and whether it was derived from the HTML), raw MIME and attachment names — or the exception it threw. PreviewController now uses it. A failure while rendering the MIME message is now reported on the preview detail page like a build failure, instead of an error response (#53).
  • Resend transport (resend mailer): delivers through the Resend HTTP API with the mailer's key, maps metadata onto Resend tags, carries attachments and inline images (content_id), and returns the Resend message id. Error responses become SendResult::fail() with Resend's message. Return path, non-default priority, and tags outside [A-Za-z0-9_-] are dropped and logged at debug.

  • HTTP client seam for API transports: HttpClientInterface returning a minimal HttpResponse, with CurlHttpClient (the default) and Psr18HttpClient (adapts any PSR-18 client plus PSR-17 factories), resolved through the overridable postalHttpClient service. AbstractApiTransport holds the shared request / JSON / error handling.

  • Markdown Mailables: author an email body as CommonMark markdown via the markdown() global helper or Mailable::markdown($view, $data), which resolves a view to raw markdown, converts it (service('markdown'), a MarkdownRenderer built from a League\CommonMark Environment), wraps the result in a shared Layout (LayoutRenderer, single-slot, applied after conversion — falls back to Config\Postal::$defaultLayout, or overridden per-Mailable with Mailable::layout()), and inlines the Layout's CSS for email-client compatibility. Also derives a plain-text fallback directly from the markdown source (MarkdownString::text()) rather than reverse-engineering it from HTML. Ships two pre-styled Mail Components — <mail-button url="..."> and <mail-panel color="..."> — resolved by a real CommonMark parser/renderer extension (MailComponentExtension), not regex or DOM post-processing. Adds league/commonmark and tijsverkoyen/css-to-inline-styles as hard dependencies. ViewPublisher, discovered and run by spark publish alongside ConfigPublisher, copies the default Layout and Mail Component views into app/Views/mail/, never overwriting existing files, so host apps can restyle them freely. Raw-HTML passthrough stays at its default throughout, so markdown views inherit CI4's usual esc()-it-yourself trust model; see Markdown Mailables. make:mailable gains a --markdown flag that scaffolds a starter markdown view alongside a build() calling ->markdown() instead of ->html().

  • spark publish writes app/Config/Mailer.php, a Config\Mailer extending the package's config, which Postal then resolves in preference to its own default. Re-running publish never overwrites an existing file.

  • Failover transport (failover mailer): a composite that tries an ordered list of child mailers (named under a chain key) and falls through to the next on failure — returning the first success and reporting failure only when every child fails. A child that throws is treated as a failure so the chain advances. MailerManager resolves the child mailers by name and hands the already-built transports to the composite. A failover mailer with no children throws a PostalException.

  • Automatic inline images: the renderer scans the HTML body for <img> sources and embeds the embeddable ones — data: image URIs (decoded in memory) and local image file paths (read at render) — rewriting each reference to a cid: URL and de-duplicating identical sources. Remote (http(s)://) and existing cid: sources are left untouched, and only files that sniff as images are read. On by default; disable per message with Email::$autoEmbedImages = false. Adds Attachment::embedData().
  • Amazon SES transport (ses mailer): delivers through the official aws/aws-sdk-php SesV2 client (SigV4 signing and HTTP owned by the SDK). Sends structured Simple content by default and switches to raw MIME for attachments/inline images, HTML without an explicit text body, or when forceRaw is set. Maps Email::metadata() onto SES EmailTags (dropping and debug-logging tags that break SES's character rules), applies an optional configurationSet, and returns the SES message id. aws/aws-sdk-php is an optional dependency (install it with composer require aws/aws-sdk-php).
  • Email::metadata(key, value) builder for provider tags, mapped by API transports onto their tagging feature and ignored by the others.
  • Attachments and inline images: Email::attach() (file by path, read lazily at render), Email::attachData() (raw bytes), and Email::embedImage() (inline CID image referenceable from HTML), backed by the Attachment value object. The renderer nests multipart/mixed (attachments) around multipart/related (inline images) around the existing multipart/alternative, with base64 parts chunked at 76 columns and part headers sanitised against filename injection.
  • Core send pipeline: compose an Email and send it through a transport via service('mailer'), receiving a SendResult.
  • Email message builder with from/replyTo/to/cc/bcc/subject/html/text/ header/priority/returnPath (mutable, chainable).
  • Address value object that parses and renders "Name <email>".
  • SendResult with ok()/fail()/cancelled() factories.
  • TransportInterface and the NullTransport implementation.
  • MailerManager (resolves the default and named mailers from Config\Mailer via an extensible transport map, lazily and cached) and a minimal Mailer that clones the message at the dispatch boundary.
  • Config\Mailer configuration and the service('mailer') service.
  • MessageRenderer that serialises an Email into a raw RFC 5322 / MIME string: text/plain, or multipart/alternative whenever HTML is present (with an automatically generated HTML→text fallback when no text body is set). Emits custom headers, Return-Path/Sender, and non-default X-Priority; applies RFC 2047 header encoding and quoted-printable body encoding (7-bit clean, within the 998-octet SMTP limit); strips CR/LF to prevent header injection; exposes the rendered header set via headers().
  • LogTransport and the built-in log mailer, which render the message and write the full MIME to a PSR-3 log channel (default level debug) instead of delivering it.
  • Email lifecycle events fired around every send: email.composing (at the start), email.sending (immediately before the transport — returning false cancels the send and yields SendResult::cancelled()), and email.sent / email.failed afterwards (each receiving the Email and SendResult). All emission is gated behind Config\Mailer::$fireEvents (default true).
  • SendmailTransport/MailTransport and the sendmail and mail mailers, which hand the rendered MIME to a local MTA: sendmail pipes it to the configured binary (path) with -oi -t, and mail splits it across PHP's native mail(). Both deliver Bcc via a header the MTA strips, set the envelope sender (-f) from the return path or From (validated and shell-escaped), and talk through the SendmailProcess/MailFunction seams for testing.
  • LegacyEmailAdapter, a drop-in replacement for CodeIgniter 4's email service. service('email') now returns the adapter, which exposes the full legacy fluent API (setFrom/setTo/setCC/setBCC/setSubject/setMessage/ setAltMessage/setMailType/setHeader/setPriority/setWordWrap/ setProtocol/attach/send/printDebugger/batchBCCSend/validation helpers) on top of the new Email builder and Mailer. Honors the legacy flat Config\Email keys (protocol, SMTP*, mailPath, mailType, wordWrap/wrapChars, priority, BCCBatch*, DSN) so existing apps need no configuration changes. Invalid addresses are swallowed (send() returns false and never throws). For CI4 parity, Return-Path and Reply-To default to From, and sends flow through the event pipeline (a email.sending listener can cancel). See Legacy Compatibility.
  • Optional hard word-wrap for the plain-text part: set Email::$wordWrap (and $wrapChars, default 76) and MessageRenderer wraps at word boundaries, leaving long space-less tokens (e.g. URLs) intact.
  • Mailer::fake() and the FakeTransport test double: swaps the bound service('mailer') for an in-memory recorder (no network, no real transport) and returns it. Exposes content-matcher assertions — assertSent(), assertSentTo(), assertNotSent(), assertNothingSent(), assertSentCount() — and sent() for inspecting the recorded messages. See Testing Mail.
  • Mailable, an abstract class-based email definition: compose the message in build() (which runs lazily at send time) via protected from/to/subject/ html/text helpers, pick a named mailer with transport(), and send() to route through service('mailer'). Each send tags the message with the Mailable's class. The make:mailable Spark command scaffolds a class into app/Mails/ (--force overwrites). FakeTransport::sent() and assertSent() now also accept a Mailable class-string (with an optional closure filter) so tests can assert by type. See Mailables.

docs.title: CLI Commands
docs.text: Postal ships a couple of spark commands to speed up everyday work. This page covers email:test; the generator for Mailables lives with the feature it scaffolds.

docs.title: email:test
docs.text:
Sends a real test message through a mailer so you can confirm a transport is configured and reachable. It runs the full pipeline — lifecycle events, suppression, and the transport itself — then prints the provider message id on success or the error on failure.

php spark email:test you@example.com

Sent. Message ID: <abc123@mail.example.com>

This sends for real

Unlike Mailer::fake(), email:test hands the message to the configured transport. Point it at a safe mailer (the log or null mailer) while you're poking around, and switch to your live mailer only when you mean to deliver.

docs.title: Choosing a mailer
docs.text:
By default the message goes through your configured default mailer. Pass --mailer (or its alias --transport) to pick a named mailer from Config\Mailer:

php spark email:test you@example.com --mailer smtp

Space, not =

CodeIgniter's spark options are space-separated. Use --mailer smtp, not --mailer=smtp.

docs.title: Prompting for the recipient
docs.text:
Leave the address off and the command asks for it:

php spark email:test

Recipient address: you@example.com

docs.title: Where the From address comes from
docs.text:
email:test reads the From address from the framework's Config\Email — fromEmail and fromName. If fromEmail is empty, it falls back to sending from the recipient address so the message always has a valid sender.

<?php

// app/Config/Email.php
public string $fromEmail = 'postmaster@example.com';
public string $fromName  = 'Example App';

docs.title: On failure
docs.text:
When the transport reports a failure, the command prints the error and exits non-zero, so it plays nicely in scripts and CI:

Send failed: Connection refused (smtp.example.com:587)

docs.title: Writing a Custom Transport
docs.text:
When Postal doesn't support your provider, write a transport for it. A transport is one class; register it in Config\Mailer and it works with mailers, events, suppression, failover and Mailer::fake() like the built-in ones.

This guide builds two:

  • EmlFileTransport writes each message to an .eml file, which is handy in development. It shows a transport that delivers the rendered email.
  • AcmeTransport sends to an HTTP JSON API. Acme Mail is made up; swap in your provider's endpoint and fields.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
A transport implements Myth\Postal\Transport\TransportInterface:

Method What it must do send(Email $email): SendResult Deliver the message. Return SendResult::ok() or SendResult::fail(). ping(): bool Return true when the transport can deliver right now, for example when the server is reachable.

Three rules keep it working with the rest of Postal:

  • Return fail(), don't throw, when the message is rejected. Throw a PostalException only for configuration problems, such as a missing API key. A failover mailer treats both as a failure and moves on.
  • Take the mailer entry as the first constructor argument. Postal builds the transport with new YourTransport($settings), where $settings is the whole mailer entry from Config\Mailer.
  • Take what you need to fake as an optional second argument, such as an HTTP client or a directory. Postal never passes it, so it's free for tests.

docs.title: A transport that writes .eml files
docs.text:
<?php

namespace App\Mail;

use Myth\Postal\Email;
use Myth\Postal\MessageRenderer;
use Myth\Postal\SendResult;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\RawMimeTransport;

final readonly class EmlFileTransport implements RawMimeTransport
{
    private string $directory;

    /**
     * @param array<string, mixed> $settings accepts an optional "directory" key
     */
    public function __construct(array $settings = [], ?string $directory = null)
    {
        $this->directory = $directory ?? (string) ($settings['directory'] ?? WRITEPATH . 'mail');
    }

    public function send(Email $email): SendResult
    {
        if (! is_dir($this->directory) && ! mkdir($this->directory, 0775, true)) {
            return SendResult::fail('Could not create ' . $this->directory);
        }

        $renderer = new MessageRenderer();

        // A DKIM-signed message arrives already rendered; send those bytes unchanged.
        $message = $email->rawMessage ?? $renderer->render($email);

        $file = $this->directory . '/' . date('Ymd-His') . '-' . bin2hex(random_bytes(4)) . '.eml';

        if (file_put_contents($file, $message) === false) {
            return SendResult::fail('Could not write ' . $file);
        }

        return SendResult::ok($renderer->headers()['Message-ID'] ?? null, $file);
    }

    public function ping(): bool
    {
        return is_dir($this->directory) && is_writable($this->directory);
    }
}

MessageRenderer turns the Email into a complete MIME message: headers, the plain-text fallback, attachments and inline images. See MIME Rendering.

Implementing RawMimeTransport instead of TransportInterface tells Postal the transport delivers the rendered message unchanged. That makes DKIM signing available to it: the signer renders and signs the message, then passes it in $email->rawMessage, which the transport must send as is. Only implement RawMimeTransport if you honour rawMessage.

docs.title: A transport for an HTTP API
docs.text:
For a JSON API, extend Myth\Postal\Transport\AbstractApiTransport. It sends the request, encodes the JSON, embeds inline images, and turns the response into a SendResult. You supply the provider-specific parts:

<?php

namespace App\Mail;

use Myth\Postal\Address;
use Myth\Postal\Email;
use Myth\Postal\Exceptions\PostalException;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\AbstractApiTransport;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\HttpClientInterface;

final readonly class AcmeTransport extends AbstractApiTransport
{
    private string $token;

    /**
     * @param array<string, mixed> $settings
     */
    public function __construct(array $settings = [], ?HttpClientInterface $http = null)
    {
        $this->token = (string) ($settings['token'] ?? '');

        if ($this->token === '') {
            throw PostalException::forMissingSetting('token', 'acme');
        }

        parent::__construct($http);
    }

    protected function endpoint(): string
    {
        return 'https://api.acme-mail.example/v1/send';
    }

    protected function headers(): array
    {
        return ['Authorization' => 'Bearer ' . $this->token];
    }

    protected function payload(Email $email): array
    {
        return [
            'from'    => $email->from instanceof Address ? $this->formatAddress($email->from) : '',
            'to'      => array_map($this->formatAddress(...), $email->to),
            'subject' => $email->subject,
            'html'    => $email->htmlBody,
            'text'    => $email->textBody,
            'tags'    => $this->supportedMetadata($email, '/^[a-z0-9_]{1,64}$/', 'lowercase letters, digits and underscores only'),
        ];
    }

    protected function messageId(array $data): ?string
    {
        return isset($data['id']) ? (string) $data['id'] : null;
    }

    protected function errorMessage(array $data): ?string
    {
        return isset($data['error']) ? (string) $data['error'] : null;
    }
}
Method Returns endpoint() The URL the message is POSTed to. headers() Request headers, usually authentication. Content-Type and Accept are added for you. payload(Email $email) The request body, as an array. messageId(array $data) The provider's message ID from a successful response. errorMessage(array $data) The provider's error from a failed response, or null to report the HTTP status.

The base class also gives you three helpers:

  • formatAddress() formats an Address as "Name" <email>, encoding non-ASCII names.
  • supportedMetadata() keeps the metadata() tags that match your provider's rules, and drops and logs the rest.
  • dropUnsupported() logs a feature the provider can't carry, such as a custom return path, instead of failing the send.

Keep the class readonly

AbstractApiTransport is a readonly class, and PHP requires its subclasses to be readonly too. Leaving it out is a fatal error.

Requests go through the postalHttpClient service, which uses cURL by default. To use your own HTTP client, see HTTP clients.

docs.title: Register it
docs.text:
Add the class to $transports and point a mailer at it in app/Config/Mailer.php. Redeclaring $transports replaces the package's map, so copy the built-in entries from Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer as well:

<?php

public array $transports = [
    // ...the built-in entries...
    'eml'  => \App\Mail\EmlFileTransport::class,
    'acme' => \App\Mail\AcmeTransport::class,
];

public array $mailers = [
    'eml'  => ['transport' => 'eml'],
    'acme' => ['transport' => 'acme'],
    // ...
];

public function __construct()
{
    parent::__construct();

    $this->mailers['acme']['token'] = env('ACME_TOKEN');
}

The new mailers work everywhere the built-in ones do: service('mailer')->mailer('acme'), $default, Mailable::transport(), and a failover chain.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
Pass the test double as the second constructor argument. For the file transport, a temporary directory:

<?php

$dir    = sys_get_temp_dir() . '/eml-' . bin2hex(random_bytes(4));
$result = (new EmlFileTransport([], $dir))->send($email);

$this->assertTrue($result->success);
$this->assertFileExists($result->raw);

For the API transport, an HttpClientInterface that records the request and returns a canned response:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Transport\HttpClientInterface;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\HttpResponse;

$http = new class () implements HttpClientInterface {
    public string $body = '';

    public function request(string $method, string $url, array $headers = [], string $body = ''): HttpResponse
    {
        $this->body = $body;

        return new HttpResponse(200, '{"id":"msg-1"}');
    }
};

$result = (new AcmeTransport(['token' => 'test'], $http))->send($email);

$this->assertSame('msg-1', $result->messageId);

Return new HttpResponse(422, '{"error":"Invalid recipient"}') to test the failure path. To check what your application sends, rather than the transport, use Mailer::fake().

docs.title: DKIM Signing
docs.text:
A DKIM signature is how a receiving server knows the message really came from your domain and wasn't tampered with in transit. It's also one of the things DMARC checks before deciding whether your mail lands in the inbox or the spam folder. Postal can sign messages for you at the library level — the signature is computed as the message is sent and travels with it.

You enable it by adding one dkim block to a mailer. The transport renders the message, signs it, and hands the signed bytes straight to delivery. There's nothing to call at send time and nothing to change in your application code.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Add a dkim key to any SMTP or sendmail mailer. It takes three values: the domain you're signing as, the selector that names the public key in DNS, and the privateKey used to sign:

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'primary' => [
        'transport'  => 'smtp',
        'host'       => 'smtp.example.com',
        'port'       => 587,
        // plus credentials — see the SMTP mailer
        'dkim'       => [
            'domain'     => 'example.com',
            'selector'   => 'postal',
            'privateKey' => WRITEPATH . 'keys/dkim-private.pem',
        ],
    ],
];

privateKey accepts either a path to a readable PEM file (as above) or the PEM text itself — handy when the key comes from an environment variable or a secrets manager. PHP doesn't allow function calls in property defaults, so set it in the config's constructor:

<?php

public function __construct()
{
    parent::__construct();

    $this->mailers['primary']['dkim']['privateKey'] = env('DKIM_PRIVATE_KEY');
}

Protect the private key

The signing key is a secret. Never paste the PEM text inline into Config\Mailer (it's committed to version control) — point privateKey at a key file kept outside your repository, or load the PEM from .env/a secrets manager via env(). Restrict the key file's permissions to the web user (for example chmod 600).

The matching public key lives in DNS as a TXT record at <selector>._domainkey.<domain> — for the example above, postal._domainkey.example.com. Until that record is published, receivers can't verify the signature, so set up DNS before you switch signing on.

A dkim block that's missing its domain, selector, or a usable privateKey is a configuration error: the mailer throws a PostalException the first time it's resolved, rather than sending unsigned mail and hoping you notice.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When you send through a signed mailer, the transport:

  1. Renders the message to its raw MIME form once.
  2. Computes a relaxed/relaxed, rsa-sha256 signature over the standard header set (From, To, Cc, Subject, Date, Message-ID, and the MIME headers) plus a hash of the body.
  3. Prepends the resulting DKIM-Signature header.
  4. Delivers those exact bytes — verbatim.

That last point is the important one. The signature covers the precise bytes of the headers and body, so the message can't be re-rendered after signing or the signature breaks. Postal signs once and the transport transmits what was signed, which is why signing is built into the delivery path rather than bolted on as a separate step.

Sign last, deliver unchanged

A DKIM signature is only valid for the message as it was signed. If something downstream rewrites the body — a relay that injects a footer, a mailing-list manager that adds an unsubscribe block — the signature no longer matches and verification fails. Library-level signing works precisely because Postal is the last thing to touch the message before it goes on the wire.

docs.title: Raw-MIME transports only
docs.text:
DKIM signing is available on the transports that deliver raw MIME and can carry the signed bytes untouched: smtp and sendmail.

It is not available on ses, resend, mail, null, or log. Adding a dkim block to one of those raises a PostalException when the mailer is resolved:

<?php

'broken' => [
    'transport' => 'ses',
    'dkim'      => ['domain' => 'example.com', 'selector' => 'postal', 'privateKey' => '...'],
],
// PostalException: The "ses" transport cannot DKIM-sign: it does not deliver
// raw MIME (such providers sign server-side). Remove the "dkim" config…

This isn't a missing feature — it's the right boundary. Amazon SES, Resend and similar API providers sign outbound mail on their own infrastructure once you've set up the DKIM records in their console. Signing the message a second time in Postal would be redundant at best and conflicting at worst. Let the provider own signing for those transports, and use Postal's signing for the ones that hand raw MIME to an MTA.

docs.title: With the failover mailer
docs.text:
DKIM is applied per leaf. A failover mailer is just a coordinator — it never renders or delivers a message itself — so it stays signing-agnostic. Each child that needs signing carries its own dkim block:

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'relay-a' => [
        'transport' => 'smtp',
        'host'      => 'smtp-a.example.com',
        'dkim'      => [
            'domain'     => 'example.com',
            'selector'   => 'postal',
            'privateKey' => WRITEPATH . 'keys/dkim-private.pem',
        ],
    ],
    'relay-b' => [
        'transport' => 'smtp',
        'host'      => 'smtp-b.example.com',
        'dkim'      => [
            'domain'     => 'example.com',
            'selector'   => 'postal',
            'privateKey' => WRITEPATH . 'keys/dkim-private.pem',
        ],
    ],
    'primary' => [
        'transport' => 'failover',
        'chain'     => ['relay-a', 'relay-b'],
    ],
];

Each leaf signs itself

Whichever child actually delivers the message signs it on the way out, so a message that falls through from relay-a to relay-b is signed by relay-b. List a dkim block on every leaf that should send signed mail; a leaf without one sends unsigned, even inside a signed chain.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• SMTP — the most common home for a dkim block
  • Sendmail & Mail — sign through a local sendmail binary
  • Failover — sign each leaf of a resilient chain

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Postal fires an event at each step of a send. They're hooks: a place to log delivery, tweak a message just before it goes out, audit failures, or stop a send entirely. If you've used CodeIgniter's event system before, this works exactly the same way.

docs.title: The four events
docs.text:
Every send walks through these in order:

Event When it fires Listener receives email.composing At the very start, before anything else Email $message email.sending Immediately before the transport runs Email $message email.sent After a successful delivery Email $message, SendResult $result email.failed After the transport reports a failure Email $message, SendResult $result

A send fires composing, then sending, then exactly one of sent or failed. If you've set up a suppression list, Postal also fires email.suppressed for each recipient it removes, between composing and sending. The $message passed to your listeners is Postal's working copy — a clone made at the start of the send — so changes you make to the original after calling send() never sneak in.

docs.title: Listening for an event
docs.text:
Register a listener with CodeIgniter's Events::on(), usually in your app's app/Config/Events.php:

<?php

use CodeIgniter\Events\Events;
use Myth\Postal\Email;
use Myth\Postal\SendResult;

Events::on('email.sent', static function (Email $message, SendResult $result): void {
    log_message('info', 'Mail sent to {to}, id {id}', [
        'to' => $message->to[0]->email,
        'id' => $result->messageId,
    ]);
});

The sent and failed listeners get the SendResult too, so you can record the provider message ID on success or the error on failure:

<?php

Events::on('email.failed', static function (Email $message, SendResult $result): void {
    log_message('error', 'Mail failed: {error}', ['error' => $result->error]);
});

docs.title: Knowing which Mailable sent it
docs.text:
When a Mailable sends the message, $message->mailableClass holds the Mailable's fully-qualified class name. Messages you build with new Email(), or send through the legacy adapter, carry null. Postal never writes this value into the email's headers, so it stays on your side of the wire:

<?php

Events::on('email.sent', static function (Email $message, SendResult $result): void {
    log_message('info', '{mailable} sent, id {id}', [
        'mailable' => $message->mailableClass ?? 'ad-hoc email',
        'id'       => $result->messageId,
    ]);
});

docs.title: Modifying the message
docs.text:
composing and sending listeners receive the live message object, so anything you change there goes out with the email. It's the clean place to enforce app-wide rules — add a compliance BCC, stamp a header, or set a default from:

<?php

Events::on('email.composing', static function (Email $message): void {
    $message->bcc('archive@example.com');
    $message->header('X-App-Version', '2.4.0');
});

Use composing for broad defaults and sending for last-second changes — the message is identical in both, so reach for whichever reads better.

docs.title: Cancelling a send
docs.text:
Return false from an email.sending listener to abort delivery. The transport is never called, and send() returns a cancelled result:

<?php

Events::on('email.sending', static function (Email $message): bool {
    if (str_ends_with($message->to[0]->email, '@blocked.example')) {
        return false; // stop the send
    }

    return true;
});

The caller sees this in the result:

<?php

$result = service('mailer')->send($email);

if ($result->cancelled) {
    // a listener stopped it — $result->success is false, nothing was sent
}

Only sending can cancel

Returning false from composing, sent, or failed does nothing — those events are notifications. Cancellation is deliberately limited to sending, the moment right before delivery.

docs.title: Turning events off
docs.text:
Events fire on every send by default. To silence all of them, including email.suppressed, set $fireEvents to false in your Config\Mailer:

<?php

public bool $fireEvents = false;

With events off, no listeners run — including any sending listener that would have cancelled — and the message goes straight to the transport. Reach for this when you want a guaranteed-clean send path (a bulk job, say) with zero listener overhead or interference.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Log — see a full message without sending it
  • MIME Rendering — what the message looks like on the wire

docs.title: Failover
docs.text:
A single provider is a single point of failure. When your primary mail service has a bad five minutes — an API outage, a throttle, a connection that won't open — the messages queued behind it don't care whose fault it is; they just don't go out. The failover transport is the answer: it wraps an ordered list of other mailers and tries them one after another, handing the message to the next as soon as one fails. The first success wins, and only an across-the-board failure is reported as a failure.

It composes mailers you've already defined, so each child keeps its own transport and settings. Point it at your SES mailer first and an SMTP relay second, and a primary outage falls through to the backup without your application noticing.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Define the child mailers as usual, then add a failover mailer that lists them by name, in priority order, under a chain key:

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'ses' => [
        'transport' => 'ses',
        'region'    => 'us-east-1',
    ],
    'backup-smtp' => [
        'transport' => 'smtp',
        'host'      => 'smtp.example.com',
        'port'      => 587,
        // plus credentials — see the SMTP mailer
    ],
    'primary' => [
        'transport' => 'failover',
        'chain'     => ['ses', 'backup-smtp'],
    ],
];

Send through it by name, exactly like any other mailer:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com', 'Your Name')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Welcome aboard')
    ->html('<p>Glad to have you with us.</p>');

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('primary')->send($email);

The children are resolved by name, so each one is built with its own settings — including any decoration it would normally receive. A failover mailer is just a coordinator; it never renders or delivers a message itself.

Make it the default

Set public string $default = 'primary'; in your Config\Mailer to route every service('mailer')->send($email) call through the failover chain without naming it each time.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Sending walks the chain list in order:

  1. The message is handed to the first child.
  2. If that child reports success, the result is returned immediately — later children are never tried.
  3. If the child reports failure or throws (a connection that won't open, a misconfigured client), the failover catches it and advances to the next child.
  4. Only when every child has failed does the failover itself report failure.

That a thrown error is treated as just another failure is deliberate: a provider whose client blows up mid-send is exactly the case you want to fall through, not a crash that takes the whole send down.

docs.title: When the whole chain fails
docs.text:
If no child succeeds, you get a single failed SendResult whose error rolls up what each child reported, so you can see why every attempt fell through:

<?php

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('primary')->send($email);

if (! $result->success) {
    log_message('error', $result->error);
    // e.g. "All failover transports failed: ses timed out; smtp auth rejected"
}

A failover mailer must list at least one child. An entry with a missing or empty chain key is a configuration error and throws a PostalException the first time the mailer is resolved, rather than silently sending nothing.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The transport composes plain TransportInterface instances, so in a unit test you can construct it directly with whatever children you need — including doubles that simulate a primary outage:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Transport\FailoverTransport;

$failover = new FailoverTransport([
    $aTransportThatFails,    // primary is down
    $aTransportThatSucceeds, // backup takes over
]);

$result = $failover->send($email);
$this->assertTrue($result->success);

The constructor takes only the ordered children; the failover renders and delivers nothing itself, so it needs no settings of its own.

docs.text:

  • SMTP — a natural backup relay
  • Testing — assert on sent messages without a live provider

docs.title: How Postal Works
docs.text: You can send mail with Postal without reading this page. It's here for when config keys, events or failures don't behave the way you expect, and you want to know what's happening underneath.

docs.title: Messages, transports and mailers
docs.text:
Postal separates three things that CodeIgniter's Email class keeps in one object:

  • An Email is what to send: addresses, subject, bodies, headers, attachments. It knows nothing about delivery.
  • A transport is how a message is delivered: over SMTP, through a sendmail binary, as a JSON request to an API, into a log. Each transport is a class implementing TransportInterface.
  • A mailer is a named transport with its settings, wrapped in the send pipeline described below. smtp, marketing and backup could all be mailers, and two of them could use the same transport with different servers.

That's why your config lists $mailers while the classes are called transports. You choose a mailer by name; the mailer decides which transport does the work.

docs.title: From config to a mailer
docs.text:
service('mailer') returns the MailerManager. When you ask it for a mailer, by name or the default, it:

  1. Looks up the entry in Config\Mailer::$mailers.
  2. Finds that entry's transport in $transports and builds the class, passing it the whole mailer entry as its settings. Each transport reads the keys it understands and ignores the rest.
  3. Wraps the transport in a mailer, together with your $fireEvents, suppression list and unsubscribe settings.
  4. Caches the mailer by name, so later calls get the same instance. That's what lets SMTP keep-alive reuse one connection across a batch.

Two kinds of entry are built differently:

  • A failover mailer builds each mailer named in its chain the same way, and wraps them in a transport that tries them in order.
  • A mailer with a dkim block has its transport wrapped in a signer, which signs the rendered message before handing it on.

Nothing is built until you first use a mailer, so a configuration mistake, such as an unknown transport or a missing API key, throws then rather than when your app boots.

docs.title: What happens during a send
docs.text:
Every send through a mailer follows the same steps:

send($email)
  │
  ├─ 1. clone the message
  ├─ 2. email.composing
  ├─ 3. suppression list ── email.suppressed per removed recipient
  │                       └─ nobody left? → cancelled
  ├─ 4. List-Unsubscribe header
  ├─ 5. email.sending ───── a listener returned false? → cancelled
  ├─ 6. transport: render → sign → deliver
  └─ 7. email.sent or email.failed → SendResult
  1. Clone. Postal works on a copy, so changing your Email after send() can't affect what goes out, and a listener's changes never leak back into your object.
  2. email.composing. The first event, for app-wide defaults such as an archive Bcc.
  3. Suppression. Runs after composing, so recipients a listener added are filtered too. If every recipient is removed, the send stops with a cancelled result and the transport is never called.
  4. Unsubscribe header. Added only for a single To recipient and only when you haven't set one. It comes after suppression, so it's never generated for an address that won't receive the message.
  5. email.sending. The last point to change or stop the message. It is the only event that can cancel, because it's the only one that runs when the message is final but not yet sent.
  6. Transport. The transport turns the message into whatever it delivers and sends it. See below.
  7. Result. email.sent or email.failed fires with the SendResult, which is then returned to you.

With $fireEvents off, steps 2, 5 and 7 fire nothing, so no listener can cancel or change the message. Suppression and the unsubscribe header still run.

docs.title: Two kinds of transport
docs.text:
Transports fall into two groups, and which group a transport is in decides what it can do.

Raw-MIME transports, such as smtp, sendmail, mail and log, turn the message into a complete email with MessageRenderer and pass on those exact bytes. Postal controls every header and part, so:

  • Postal generates the plain-text part when you only set HTML.
  • DKIM signing works on smtp and sendmail, because the signed bytes are the bytes delivered.
  • Provider tags from metadata() have nowhere to go, so they're ignored.

API transports, such as ses and resend, send fields to a provider's HTTP API, and the provider builds the email. So:

  • The provider signs the message with its own DKIM keys, and a dkim block is a configuration error.
  • metadata() becomes the provider's tags.
  • Anything the provider can't carry, such as a custom return path on Resend, is dropped and logged rather than failing the send.

docs.title: Mailables and the legacy adapter
docs.text:
Both end up in the same pipeline:

  • A Mailable builds an Email in build() and sends it through service('mailer'), tagging it with its class name.
  • service('email') returns the legacy adapter, which turns CodeIgniter-style calls such as setTo() and setMessage() into an Email. Once you've published Config\Mailer, it sends through your default mailer like everything else.

So events, suppression and transports behave the same whichever way a message was written.

docs.title: How failures surface
docs.text:
Postal separates three kinds of "it didn't go":

What happened What you get The server or provider rejected the message SendResult with success false and an error A listener or the suppression list stopped it SendResult with cancelled true; the transport never ran The configuration is wrong (unknown mailer, missing key, bad DKIM block) A PostalException thrown when the mailer is first used

Delivery problems are values you check; configuration problems are exceptions you fix. A failover mailer relies on that: it moves to the next child on a failed result, and also on an exception, so one broken provider can't take the whole send down.

docs.text:

  • Events — hooking into the send steps above
  • Writing a Custom Transport — adding your own transport to the picture

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• PHP 8.2+
  • CodeIgniter 4.7+
  • Extensions: ext-openssl, ext-mbstring (and ext-curl for the HTTP API transports)

docs.title: Install via Composer
docs.text:
composer require myth/postal

CodeIgniter auto-discovers the package through Composer — no manual registration is required.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Transports are defined as named mailers in Config\Mailer. $default names the mailer used when you don't pick one. Out of the box it is null, which discards every message, so nothing is sent until you choose a transport:

<?php

public string $default = 'log';

public array $mailers = [
    'smtp' => [
        'transport'  => 'smtp',
        'host'       => 'localhost',
        'port'       => 587,
        'encryption' => 'tls',
    ],
    'log'  => ['transport' => 'log'],
    'null' => ['transport' => 'null'],
];

To use a different mailer in each environment, override $default from that environment's .env file:

mailer.default = smtp

To override the defaults in your application, publish the config file:

php spark publish

That writes app/Config/Mailer.php — a Config\Mailer class extending the package's Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer. Redeclare only the properties you want to change; everything else is inherited. Postal resolves the application's copy in preference to its own, so the settings you put there are the ones that take effect.

Publishing never overwrites an existing app/Config/Mailer.php, so it is safe to re-run after upgrading the package.

The same php spark publish run also copies the default email Layout and Mail Components — app/Views/mail/layouts/default.php and app/Views/mail/components/{button,panel}.php — so you can restyle them to match your brand. As with the config file, publishing never overwrites a copy you've already customized. See Markdown Mailables for what those files do.

Every property and transport setting is listed in the Config\Mailer reference.

docs.title: Verify the install
docs.text:
Once $default names a real mailer, send a test message through it:

php spark email:test you@example.com

The command runs the full send pipeline and prints the result (provider message ID, or the error if it failed). With the package default, null, it reports success without sending anything, so set $default first.

docs.title: Legacy Compatibility
docs.text:
Postal ships a drop-in replacement for CodeIgniter 4's built-in email service. Existing application code that calls service('email') keeps working unchanged — the same fluent setX API, the same send() returning a boolean — but every message now flows through Postal's Email builder, Mailer, and transports.

No configuration changes are required: the adapter reads the flat Config\Email keys your app already has. Once you publish app/Config/Mailer.php, the adapter sends through your default mailer instead (see Which mailer sends).

This page describes everything the adapter does. For a step-by-step move from CodeIgniter's Email onto Postal, see Migrating from CI4's Email.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
service('email') returns a Myth\Postal\LegacyEmailAdapter. The adapter composes a new Email value object from the legacy setters and sends it through a Mailer built from your configured protocol. The new Email itself carries none of the legacy API — the compatibility layer lives entirely in the adapter.

<?php

$email = service('email');

$email->setFrom('me@example.com', 'Me')
    ->setTo('you@example.com')
    ->setSubject('Hello')
    ->setMessage('Plain text body');

if (! $email->send()) {
    log_message('error', $email->printDebugger(['headers']));
}

docs.title: Which mailer sends
docs.text:
The adapter picks its transport by asking one question: has the app configured Postal?

  • No app/Config/Mailer.php. The adapter builds a transport from the flat Config\Email keys, as described in Legacy configuration keys.
  • An app Config\Mailer exists (any subclass of Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer, such as the one php spark publish writes). The adapter sends through the default mailer, service('mailer')->mailer(). The flat transport keys (protocol, mailPath, SMTP*, DSN) are ignored, including keys passed to initialize() or setProtocol(). Shield's emailer() always passes them, and its mail still goes through your default mailer.

Message keys (mailType, wordWrap/wrapChars, priority, BCCBatchMode/BCCBatchSize, fromEmail/fromName) apply either way. When the default mailer handles the send, its fireEvents, suppression list and unsubscribe settings apply too.

Behaviour change

Before, publishing Config\Mailer had no effect on service('email'), which kept sending through Config\Email (usually PHP's mail()). If you publish Config\Mailer, make sure its default mailer is the one your legacy mail should use. LegacyConfigMapper can turn your Config\Email settings into a mailer definition.

docs.title: Type compatibility and Shield
docs.text:
LegacyEmailAdapter extends CodeIgniter\Email\Email. Code that type-hints the framework class accepts it, so CodeIgniter Shield's emailer() helper works with no changes. Activation, two-factor, and magic-link emails all send through Postal's transports and fire Postal's events (unless your Config\Mailer turns fireEvents off).

The framework class is used only for its type. The adapter never runs the parent constructor, and it overrides every method that builds or sends a message. The framework's own sender is never used. See ADR 0002.

Set options through the setters or initialize(). The adapter inherits the framework's public properties ($mailType, $SMTPHost, …), but writing them directly is not supported.

If you subclass the adapter, your overrides must match the framework's untyped parameters. For example, write setFrom($from, $name = '', $returnPath = null), not setFrom(string $from, ...).

docs.title: Supported methods
docs.text:
The full legacy surface is available:

Area Methods Composition setFrom($from, $name, $returnPath), setReplyTo, setTo, setCC, setBCC($bcc, $limit), setSubject, setMessage, setAltMessage, setHeader, setPriority Body type setMailType('text'\|'html') governs whether setMessage fills the HTML or text part; setAltMessage sets the plain-text alternative for an HTML message Behaviour setProtocol('mail'\|'sendmail'\|'smtp'), setWordWrap, setNewline/setCRLF (accepted, no-op), initialize(array $config), clear($clearAttachments) Send / debug send($autoClear) returns bool, batchBCCSend(), printDebugger($include) Postal additions lastResult() returns the SendResult of the most recent send, and lastEmail() the Email that was sent. Both are null before the first send. With BCC batch mode they hold the last batch. Validation validateEmail, isValidEmail, cleanEmail

setMessage order-independence is preserved: whether you call setMailType('html') before or after setMessage, the body lands in the right part because the choice is resolved at send time.

docs.title: Legacy configuration keys
docs.text:
When the app has not published Config\Mailer, the adapter maps your existing app/Config/Email.php onto the new mailer:

  • protocol selects the transport (mail, sendmail, or smtp) for the send. It is case-insensitive, and an unknown value falls back to mail.
  • SMTPHost, SMTPUser, SMTPPass, SMTPPort, SMTPTimeout, SMTPCrypto, SMTPKeepAlive, and SMTPAuthMethod configure the SMTP transport. Auth is enabled automatically when a username and password are both set.
  • mailPath is the sendmail binary path.
  • mailType, priority, wordWrap/wrapChars, and BCCBatchMode/BCCBatchSize seed the matching defaults.
  • DSN requests delivery-status notifications over SMTP.

initialize() merges per-call overrides on top of these without touching the shared config.

docs.title: Reusing the legacy mapping
docs.text:
Myth\Postal\LegacyConfigMapper::toMailer(array $flat): array exposes the mapping the adapter uses. Pass it the flat Config\Email keys, for example from a settings table, and it returns a mailer definition you can put in Config\Mailer::$mailers. Mail sent through that mailer goes out the same way as it would through the adapter.

use Myth\Postal\LegacyConfigMapper;

$mailer = LegacyConfigMapper::toMailer([
    'protocol' => 'smtp',
    'SMTPHost' => 'smtp.example.com',
    'SMTPPort' => '587',
    'SMTPUser' => 'user',
    'SMTPPass' => 'secret',
]);
// ['transport' => 'smtp', 'host' => 'smtp.example.com', 'port' => 587,
//  'timeout' => 5, 'encryption' => 'tls', 'keepAlive' => false,
//  'username' => 'user', 'password' => 'secret', 'authType' => 'login']
Input key Output key Default protocol transport mail mailPath path (sendmail) /usr/sbin/sendmail SMTPHost host '' SMTPPort port 25 SMTPTimeout timeout 5 SMTPCrypto encryption tls SMTPKeepAlive keepAlive false SMTPUser username '' SMTPPass password '' SMTPAuthMethod authType login DSN dsn false
  • Defaults. Missing or null keys take Config\Email's defaults shown above. Other keys are ignored.
  • Casting. Values are cast with CodeIgniter's DataCaster, the engine behind Model and Entity $casts, so database-style strings work: '587' becomes 587, and '0', 'false', '' and 'f' become false. Other keys are cast to strings.
  • Protocol. The protocol is lowercased. Anything other than smtp, sendmail or mail falls back to mail.
  • Per transport. sendmail returns only transport and path, and mail returns only transport. The SMTP keys appear only for smtp.
  • Credentials. username, password and authType are included only when SMTPUser and SMTPPass are both non-empty, so no empty credentials are passed.
  • DSN. When DSN is true, dsn is ['notify' => 'SUCCESS,FAILURE,DELAY', 'ret' => 'FULL']. Otherwise it is left out.

docs.title: Behavioural notes
docs.text:
• Invalid addresses are swallowed. Regardless of the validate setting, a malformed address is never thrown — it is recorded in the debugger and skipped, and send() returns false.
  • Header defaults match CI4. The envelope sender (Return-Path) defaults to the From address when you don't pass a return path to setFrom(), and Reply-To defaults to From when you don't set one.
  • Events fire. Adapter sends flow through Postal's event pipeline: a listener on email.sending can cancel the send (which then returns false). When your app publishes Config\Mailer, its fireEvents setting decides whether they fire.
  • BCC batch mode loops the blind recipients in BCCBatchSize chunks; the result is the logical AND of every batch.
  • printDebugger() renders the current message (headers, subject, body) through MessageRenderer and prepends any recorded errors. The output is compatible with the legacy debugger, though not byte-identical, and user-supplied values are HTML-escaped.
  • Word wrap maps to the renderer's hard wrap (see MIME Rendering).

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
attach() accepts a file path and the message is delivered with the file attached, just like the native service. setAttachmentCID() marks a previously attached file as an inline image and returns its Content-ID, so HTML bodies can reference it with a cid: URL.

An unreadable attachment path fails the send: send() returns false with an explanatory note in printDebugger() rather than throwing.

Limitation: the in-memory buffer form of CI4's attach() — passing raw file contents as the first argument together with an explicit MIME type instead of a path — is not supported. Such a value is treated as a path, found to be unreadable, and fails the send. Attach files by path instead.

docs.title: Log
docs.text: Sometimes you don't want to send real email — you just want to see what would have gone out. The built-in log mailer renders each message to its full MIME form and writes it to your application log instead of delivering it. It's perfect for local development and testing.

docs.title: Sending through the log mailer
docs.text:
Postal ships a ready-to-use log mailer. Grab it by name and send as usual:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com', 'Your Name')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Welcome aboard')
    ->html('<p>Glad to have you with us.</p>');

service('mailer')->mailer('log')->send($email);

Nothing leaves your machine. The complete message — headers and body — lands in your log file, where you can confirm the recipients, subject, and rendered MIME are exactly what you expect.

docs.title: Making it the default
docs.text:
To route all mail to the log while developing, point the default mailer at log in your Config\Mailer:

<?php

public string $default = 'log';

Now service('mailer')->send($email) logs instead of sends — no per-call changes needed.

docs.title: Choosing the log level
docs.text:
LogTransport writes at the debug level by default. That keeps full message dumps out of your production info-and-above logs. Pick a different level with the level key on the log mailer in your Config\Mailer:

<?php

'log' => ['transport' => 'log', 'level' => 'info'],

Or set it when you construct the transport yourself — settings come first as an array:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Transport\LogTransport;

$transport = new LogTransport(['level' => 'info']);

By default the transport uses CodeIgniter's shared logger (service('logger')). Pass any PSR-3 LoggerInterface as the second argument — handy for directing mail to a dedicated channel or for asserting on it in tests.

<?php

$transport = new LogTransport(['level' => 'debug'], $myPsr3Logger);

docs.title: What gets written
docs.text:
The log entry is the same raw MIME the real transports would send: the envelope and structural headers, any custom headers you added, and the encoded body (a multipart/alternative message whenever HTML is present). See MIME Rendering for the full picture.

Logs contain the full message

The log mailer writes every recipient and the entire body to your logs. Treat those logs as sensitive, and don't enable the log mailer in production unless you understand where those entries go and who can read them.

docs.text: • MIME Rendering — exactly what the logged message looks like and why

docs.title: Mailables
docs.text:
A Mailable is a reusable, class-based email. Instead of building an Email inline every time you need to send a welcome message, you describe it once in a class and send it wherever you need it.

<?php

(new WelcomeEmail($user))->send();

That's the whole idea: the message lives in one place, the call site stays a single line, and tests can assert on it by type.

docs.title: A quick example
docs.text:
A Mailable extends Myth\Postal\Mailable and composes the message in build():

<?php

namespace App\Mails;

use Myth\Postal\Mailable;

class WelcomeEmail extends Mailable
{
    public function __construct(private readonly User $user)
    {
        parent::__construct();
    }

    protected function build(): void
    {
        $this->from('hello@example.com', 'Acme')
            ->to($this->user->email, $this->user->name)
            ->subject('Welcome aboard')
            ->html(view('emails/welcome', ['user' => $this->user]))
            ->text('Glad to have you, ' . $this->user->name);
    }
}

Send it from anywhere:

<?php

$result = (new WelcomeEmail($user))->send();

send() returns the same SendResult you get from the mailer directly, so you can check $result->success if you need to.

Call the parent constructor

If your Mailable defines its own __construct(), call parent::__construct(). That's what sets up the underlying Email the helpers compose into.

docs.title: Composing in build()
docs.text:
build() is where you describe the message. It runs lazily, when you call send() or render() — never in the constructor. So passing data into the constructor and reading it in build() (like $this->user above) always works.

Build each instance once

Every send() or render() call runs build() again on the same message, so calling render() and then send() on one instance adds the recipients twice. Use a fresh instance for each.

Inside build() you have protected helpers that mirror part of the Email builder:

Helper What it sets from(string $address, string $name = '') The sender to(array\|string $address, string $name = '') A recipient (call more than once to add several) subject(string $subject) The subject line html(string $html) The HTML body text(string $text) The plain-text body markdown(string $view, array $data = []) Both bodies at once, from a markdown view — see Markdown Mailables layout(string $view) Overrides the Layout markdown() wraps its HTML in, for this Mailable only — call it before markdown() transport(string $name) The named mailer to send through — see Choosing a mailer

Each returns $this, so they chain.

For anything else, such as cc(), bcc(), replyTo(), attachments or metadata(), call the Email builder directly through the protected $this->email property:

<?php

$this->email->cc('team@example.com');

Prefer markdown() over hand-rolled html()/text()

If your body is prose rather than bespoke markup, ->markdown('emails/welcome', [...]) gets you converted HTML, a matching plain-text fallback, and a shared page layout in one call. See Markdown Mailables.

docs.title: Choosing a mailer
docs.text:
By default a Mailable sends through your default mailer. To route through a named mailer from Config\Mailer, call transport() in build():

<?php

protected function build(): void
{
    $this->transport('marketing')
        ->from('news@example.com')
        ->to($this->user->email)
        ->subject('This month at Acme')
        ->html(view('emails/newsletter', ['user' => $this->user]));
}

transport('marketing') selects the mailer named marketing — the same name you'd pass to service('mailer')->mailer('marketing').

docs.title: Generating a Mailable
docs.text:
Spark scaffolds one for you:

php spark make:mailable Welcome

That writes app/Mails/Welcome.php in the App\Mails namespace, with an empty build() ready to fill in. The generated class also implements Previewable with a previewInstance() stub, so it shows up in the browser preview out of the box. Pass --force to overwrite an existing file:

php spark make:mailable Welcome --force

Pass --markdown to scaffold a Markdown Mailable instead: alongside the class, it writes a starter markdown view at app/Views/emails/welcome.php, and generates a build() that calls ->markdown('emails/welcome') rather than ->html(''):

php spark make:mailable Welcome --markdown

--force applies to both files, independently — each is only overwritten if it already exists and --force was passed.

Pass --namespace to generate into another registered namespace, such as a module. The class lands in that namespace's Mails directory:

php spark make:mailable Welcome --namespace Acme\\Blog

Remember to add the namespace to $mailableNamespaces if you want the Mailable in the preview.

docs.title: Previewing Mailables
docs.text: Postal can render any Mailable to your browser — HTML, plain text and raw MIME — without sending it. See Previewing Mailables.

docs.title: Rendering without sending
docs.text:
The browser preview is built on Mailable::render(), a public seam you can use anywhere:

<?php

$email = (new WelcomeEmail($user))->render();

echo $email->subject;
echo $email->htmlBody;

render() runs build() and hands back the composed Email — it never sends. It's the build-without-send counterpart to send().

docs.title: Markdown Mailables
docs.text: Instead of hand-rolling HTML for every email, write the body as plain CommonMark markdown. Postal converts it to HTML, derives a plain-text fallback from that same source, wraps the result in a shared page layout, and gives you pre-styled components for things like buttons and callout panels — so your emails stay visually consistent without every mailable reinventing its own markup.

docs.title: Quick start: Mailable::markdown()
docs.text:
The fast path is a single call in your Mailable's build(): point markdown() at a view file, and it handles conversion, layout, and the plain-text fallback for you.

<?php

namespace App\Mails;

use Myth\Postal\Mailable;

class WelcomeEmail extends Mailable
{
    public function __construct(private readonly User $user)
    {
        parent::__construct();
    }

    protected function build(): void
    {
        $this->from('hello@example.com', 'Acme')
            ->to($this->user->email, $this->user->name)
            ->subject('Welcome aboard')
            ->markdown('emails/welcome', ['user' => $this->user]);
    }
}

emails/welcome is a plain CI4 view file (app/Views/emails/welcome.php) written in markdown, not HTML — headings, bold text, links, and the Mail Components below all just work. Behind the scenes, ->markdown():

  1. Resolves the view and converts it from markdown to HTML.
  2. Wraps that HTML in a Layout — a shared page template.
  3. Inlines the layout's CSS, so styling survives in email clients that strip <style> blocks.
  4. Sets both outputs on the Mailable: html() with the rendered HTML, text() with a plain-text fallback generated from the markdown source.

From the outside, a Mailable calling ->markdown(...) behaves exactly like one calling ->html()->text() directly — same Email::$htmlBody/$textBody, same Mailer::fake()/assertSent() surface.

Want a different layout for one Mailable? Call layout() before markdown():

<?php

protected function build(): void
{
    $this->from('news@example.com')
        ->to($this->user->email)
        ->subject('This month at Acme')
        ->layout('mail/layouts/marketing')
        ->markdown('emails/newsletter', ['user' => $this->user]);
}

markdown() resolves the layout the moment it runs, so layout() has to come first — call it afterward and Postal throws a Myth\Postal\Exceptions\PostalException instead of silently ignoring it.

Generate the scaffolding for you

php spark make:mailable Welcome --markdown scaffolds both the Mailable class and a starter markdown view, with build() already wired up to call ->markdown(). See Mailables.

docs.title: Mail Components
docs.text:
Mail Components are reusable, pre-styled elements you drop straight into your markdown using mail--prefixed tags. Postal ships two: a button and a panel.

<mail-button url="https://example.com/confirm">Confirm Email</mail-button>

They aren't a regex trick — Mail Component tags are parsed as real nodes in the markdown document, right alongside headings and lists. There's nothing to enable; they're always available inside any markdown view.

A tag's attributes become the component view's data, and its inner content becomes a $slot variable, so the example above resolves to:

view('mail/components/button', ['url' => 'https://example.com/confirm', 'slot' => 'Confirm Email'])

docs.title: Single-line vs. multi-line
docs.text:
Write a component two ways, depending on how much content it needs to wrap:

Single-lineMulti-line 
<mail-button url="https://example.com/confirm">Confirm Email</mail-button>

Everything between the tags is inline content — **bold**, links, and code spans all work, but nested Mail Components don't.

<mail-panel color="#fef3c7">
Heads up — your trial ends **Friday**.

[Upgrade now](https://example.com/upgrade) to keep your data.
</mail-panel>

The closing tag lives on its own line. Everything in between is parsed as full markdown, including multiple paragraphs and nested Mail Components.

Keep the closing tag clean

On a single-line tag, the closing </mail-...> has to be the last thing on the line. Write something after it — <mail-button url="...">Confirm</mail-button> and click here — and Postal won't recognize it as a Mail Component at all. It falls back to plain HTML in the markdown, tag and all.

docs.title: The shipped components
docs.text:
Component Attributes Notes <mail-button> url (required) Renders a styled link. Omitting url throws a Myth\Postal\Exceptions\PostalException with a clear message, rather than rendering a broken link. <mail-panel> color (optional) A callout box. Takes a hex value (#fef3c7) or a CSS colour keyword (linen); anything else falls back to the default light blue, since the value lands directly in a style attribute.

Both are styled with inline style="" attributes directly on their own markup, rather than relying solely on the layout's CSS inlining — so they still look right even in clients that strip <style> blocks entirely.

docs.title: Components in the plain-text part
docs.text:
The plain-text fallback can't show a button or a panel, so each component turns into plain text there. Postal drops the tags and keeps the slot content, with its lines, list items and paragraphs. If a component has a url attribute, the URL follows the slot in parentheses, the same way a markdown link does:

Confirm Email (https://example.com/confirm)

A component with an empty slot leaves just its url, or nothing if it has none. The text comes from the markdown source, not from the component's view. So anything the view adds on its own, such as fixed wording or a URL it builds from other attributes, won't be in the text. When that matters, call ->text() after ->markdown() with your own text. An explicit text() always replaces the generated one.

Want to restyle them, or add your own? Config\Postal::$componentViewPath (default 'mail/components') controls where <mail-{tag}> looks for its view — <mail-button> resolves to {componentViewPath}/button. See the tip below for copying the shipped views into your own app.

docs.title: Customizing the Layout
docs.text:
A Layout is the shared page template your markdown gets wrapped in — a single slot, filled in with the HTML your markdown converted to. It's applied after conversion, which is a deliberate difference from CodeIgniter's own extend()/section(): those compose at the raw view level, before anything's been converted, and don't give Postal a clean point to run CSS inlining or resolve Mail Components against the final HTML.

The default layout ships at mail/layouts/default, and receives the converted content as $content:

<!-- app/Views/mail/layouts/default.php -->
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; background: #f4f4f5; }
  .container { max-width: 600px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 24px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container">
    <?= $content ?>
  </div>
</body>
</html>

Make it yours

Run php spark publish to copy the default Layout and Mail Components into your app — see Installation — then edit the copies in app/Views/mail/ freely. Postal always prefers your app's version over its own, and publishing never overwrites a file you've already customized.

Mailable::markdown() uses Config\Postal::$defaultLayout (default 'mail/layouts/default') unless you override it per-Mailable with layout(), as shown in the quick start above.

The <style> block stays

CSS inlining adds style="" attributes for clients that need them, but it doesn't strip the original <style> block — clients that do render <head> styles get the benefit of both.

docs.title: Advanced: converting markdown directly
docs.text:
Mailable::markdown() covers the common case, but its two building blocks — the markdown() helper and LayoutRenderer — are useful on their own too, if you want converted HTML without the full pipeline.

The markdown() helper resolves a view file to raw markdown and converts it in one call. It's a global helper, always available — no helper() call needed, same as CodeIgniter's own view():

<?php

$rendered = markdown('emails/welcome', ['name' => $user->name]);

echo (string) $rendered;   // the converted HTML
echo $rendered->text();    // a plain-text fallback, derived from the same markdown source

If you already have a markdown string rather than a view file, call the conversion service directly:

<?php

$html = service('markdown')->toHtml('# Hello **World**');
$text = service('markdown')->toText('# Hello **World**');

Config\Postal::$markdownExtensions controls which CommonMark extensions load on top of the core parser. By default that's GitHub-Flavored Markdown (tables, strikethrough, autolinks):

<?php

public array $markdownExtensions = [
    League\CommonMark\Extension\GithubFlavoredMarkdownExtension::class,
];

To apply a Layout yourself — without going through a Mailable — use LayoutRenderer, which wraps content in a Layout and inlines its CSS:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Markdown\LayoutRenderer;

$html = (new LayoutRenderer())->render((string) $rendered);

That uses Config\Postal::$defaultLayout too, unless you pass a second argument to use a different layout for just this call:

<?php

$html = (new LayoutRenderer())->render((string) $rendered, 'mail/layouts/marketing');

docs.title: Security: raw HTML passthrough
docs.text:
CommonMark's raw-HTML passthrough is left at its default (allow): any HTML you write directly in a markdown view — including a value interpolated without esc() — reaches the rendered email unescaped, exactly as it would in a regular CI4 view.

Escape untrusted data yourself

Markdown mailables carry the same trust model as any other CodeIgniter view: nothing here sanitizes interpolated values automatically. If a markdown view interpolates data a user controls — a name, a comment, a URL — wrap it in esc() yourself, exactly as you would in a regular .php view:

<?php
// app/Views/emails/comment-notification.php
?>
New comment from **<?= esc($comment->authorName) ?>**:

> <?= esc($comment->body) ?>

Skipping this is no more or less risky than skipping esc() in an HTML view — but it's easy to assume markdown is "just text" and let your guard down. It isn't: it compiles to HTML, and unescaped interpolation compiles right along with it.

docs.title: Config reference
docs.text: The markdown settings — $markdownExtensions, $componentViewPath and $defaultLayout — are listed in the Config\Postal reference.
