docs.title: Migrating from CI4's Email
docs.text:
This guide moves an existing CodeIgniter 4 app from the framework's Email class onto Postal. It works in three stages. Each one leaves your app sending mail, so you can stop after any of them.

Stage What changes Code changes 1. Install service('email') is now Postal's adapter, still configured by Config\Email None 2. Move settings Delivery is configured in Config\Mailer Config only 3. Rewrite call sites Code uses Postal's Email or Mailables directly Optional, file by file

docs.title: Stage 1: Install
docs.text:
composer require myth/postal

That's the whole stage. service('email') now returns Postal's LegacyEmailAdapter, which accepts the same calls as CodeIgniter's Email class and reads your existing app/Config/Email.php. CodeIgniter Shield's emails keep working too.

Check that mail still goes out by sending something real through service('email'), such as a Shield password reset.

Don't use php spark email:test yet. It sends through Postal's default mailer, which is null until Stage 2, so it reports success without sending anything.

docs.title: Stage 2: Move delivery settings into Config\Mailer
docs.text:
Publish the config:

php spark publish

Publishing switches the adapter over

Once app/Config/Mailer.php exists, service('email') sends through its default mailer and ignores the delivery keys in Config\Email (protocol, SMTP*, mailPath, DSN). The package default is null, which discards mail, so set $default in the same change.

Turn your Config\Email settings into a mailer. LegacyConfigMapper does the conversion with the same rules the adapter used in Stage 1, so mail goes out exactly as before:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\LegacyConfigMapper;

print_r(LegacyConfigMapper::toMailer((array) config(\Config\Email::class)));
// ['transport' => 'smtp', 'host' => 'smtp.example.com', 'port' => 587, ...]

Copy the output into app/Config/Mailer.php and make it the default. Move the password into the constructor so it stays out of the committed file:

<?php

namespace Config;

use Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer as PostalMailer;

class Mailer extends PostalMailer
{
    public string $default = 'smtp';

    public array $mailers = [
        'smtp' => [
            'transport'  => 'smtp',
            'host'       => 'smtp.example.com',
            'port'       => 587,
            'encryption' => 'tls',
            'authType'   => 'login',
            'timeout'    => 5,
        ],
        'log'  => ['transport' => 'log'],
        'null' => ['transport' => 'null'],
    ];

    public function __construct()
    {
        parent::__construct();

        $this->mailers['smtp']['username'] = env('SMTP_USER');
        $this->mailers['smtp']['password'] = env('SMTP_PASS');
    }
}

Run php spark email:test you@example.com again. This time it goes through the same mailer as service('email').

fromEmail, fromName, mailType, wordWrap, priority and the BCC batch settings stay in Config\Email: the adapter still reads them.

docs.title: Stage 3: Rewrite call sites (optional)
docs.text:
The adapter can stay forever. Rewrite call sites when you want what Postal adds: a SendResult instead of a bool, named mailers, or Mailables you can preview and assert on by class.

Most calls map one to one:

CodeIgniter Email Postal Email setFrom($email, $name) from($email, $name) setReplyTo($email, $name) replyTo($email, $name) setTo($to) to($to) setCC($cc) / setBCC($bcc) cc($cc) / bcc($bcc) setSubject($subject) subject($subject) setMailType('html') + setMessage($body) html($body) setMessage($body) (text mail) text($body) setAltMessage($text) text($text) setHeader($name, $value) header($name, $value) setPriority($level) priority($level) attach($path) attach($path) setAttachmentCID($path) embedImage($path, $cid) send() → bool service('mailer')->send($email) → SendResult printDebugger() $result->error, or the log mailer

Before:

<?php

$email = service('email');

$email->setFrom('hello@example.com', 'Acme')
    ->setTo($user->email)
    ->setSubject('Your receipt')
    ->setMailType('html')
    ->setMessage(view('emails/receipt', ['order' => $order]));

if (! $email->send()) {
    log_message('error', $email->printDebugger(['headers']));
}

After:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('hello@example.com', 'Acme')
    ->to($user->email)
    ->subject('Your receipt')
    ->html(view('emails/receipt', ['order' => $order]));

$result = service('mailer')->send($email);

if (! $result->success) {
    log_message('error', 'Receipt failed: ' . $result->error);
}

Postal's from() and to() throw a PostalException for a malformed address, where the adapter quietly returned false from send(). Validate user-supplied addresses first, or catch the exception.

If the same message is sent from more than one place, make it a Mailable instead.

docs.title: Update your tests
docs.text:
CIUnitTestCase replaces service('email') with CodeIgniter's MockEmail before every test. Existing tests keep passing, but they never reach Postal.

To test through Postal, remove mockEmail from the test case's set-up methods and fake the mailer:

<?php

namespace Tests;

use CodeIgniter\Test\CIUnitTestCase;
use Myth\Postal\Mailer;

final class ReceiptTest extends CIUnitTestCase
{
    protected $setUpMethods = ['resetFactories', 'mockCache', 'mockSession'];

    public function testReceiptIsSent(): void
    {
        $fake = Mailer::fake();

        // ...code that sends the receipt...

        $fake->assertSentTo('customer@example.com');
    }
}

Finish Stage 2 first

Mailer::fake() only catches adapter sends once Config\Mailer is published. Before that, the adapter builds its own transport from Config\Email, so a test without mockEmail sends real mail.

See Testing for every assertion.

docs.title: What behaves differently
docs.text:
The adapter matches CodeIgniter's behaviour closely, but not exactly. The differences most likely to matter:

  • Bad addresses don't throw. A malformed address is skipped and send() returns false, whatever your validate setting.
  • No in-memory attachments. attach() with file contents instead of a path isn't supported. Write the contents to a file, or use attachData() after Stage 3.
  • Events fire. Adapter sends fire Postal's events, so an email.sending listener can cancel them.
  • Debugger output differs. printDebugger() shows the same information, but not byte for byte.

Legacy Compatibility lists everything the adapter does.

docs.title: MIME Rendering
docs.text:
MessageRenderer turns an Email into a complete, RFC 5322 / MIME message as a raw string. Transports that speak raw MIME — like the log mailer and the SMTP, sendmail and mail transports — hand their message to it. You rarely call it directly, but knowing what it produces helps you reason about what actually leaves your app.

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;
use Myth\Postal\MessageRenderer;

$mime = (new MessageRenderer())->render($email);

docs.title: Text, HTML, and the automatic fallback
docs.text:
What the renderer produces depends on which bodies you set:

  • Text only (->text(...)) → a single text/plain part.
  • Any HTML (->html(...)) → a multipart/alternative message with both a text/plain and a text/html part, in that order.

Here's the important part: whenever you set HTML but no text, the renderer generates a plain-text version for you and ships it as the text part. So an HTML email is always multipart.

Why bother? A bare text/html message with no plain-text alternative is one of the strongest spam signals there is — filters like SpamAssassin flag it outright. Generating the fallback keeps your deliverability healthy without any extra work.

The generated text is a best-effort conversion of your HTML:

  • <script>, <style>, and <head> blocks are removed whole, so their CSS, JS, and metadata never leak into the text
  • <a href="https://example.com">our site</a> becomes our site (https://example.com)
  • block-level tags (<p>, <div>, <br>, headings, list items…) become line breaks
  • remaining tags are stripped and HTML entities decoded (& → &)

Your Email is never mutated

The fallback is built at render time only. Your original Email object still has textBody === null afterward — nothing is written back.

If you want full control over the plain-text version, just set it yourself with ->text(...) and the renderer uses yours verbatim.

docs.title: Attachments and inline images
docs.text:
Three builder methods add files to a message:

<?php

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Your receipt')
    ->html('<p>Thanks! Your logo: <img src="cid:logo"></p>')
    ->attach('/path/to/receipt.pdf')                 // a file on disk
    ->attachData($bytes, 'report.csv', 'text/csv')   // raw bytes in memory
    ->embedImage('/path/to/logo.png', 'logo');       // inline image, referenced by CID
  • attach($path, $name = '', $mime = '') — attaches a file by path. The display name defaults to the file's basename and the MIME type is detected from the file; pass $name/$mime to override either.
  • attachData($data, $name, $mime = '') — attaches raw bytes you already have in memory. The MIME type defaults to application/octet-stream when omitted.
  • embedImage($path, $cid, $name = '', $mime = '') — embeds an image as an inline part. Reference it from your HTML with a cid: URL whose value matches $cid (e.g. <img src="cid:logo">).

docs.title: What gets rendered
docs.text:
The renderer only adds the containers a message actually needs, nesting them like this:

multipart/mixed              ← present when there are attachments
└── multipart/related        ← present when there are inline images
    └── multipart/alternative ← present when there is HTML
        ├── text/plain
        └── text/html

Each level appears only when it has something to hold: a text-only message with one attachment is simply multipart/mixed wrapping a text/plain part. Attachments carry Content-Disposition: attachment; inline images carry Content-Disposition: inline plus a Content-ID, and the multipart/related container names its root part with a type parameter, as RFC 2387 expects. Binary parts are base64-encoded and wrapped at 76 columns (RFC 2045).

docs.title: Lazy reads
docs.text:
Path-based attachments (attach() and embedImage()) are read from disk at render time, not when you call the method — so the file only needs to exist when the message is sent. If the file can't be read at that point, render() throws a PostalException. Bytes passed to attachData() are carried as-is.

Attach only trusted paths

attach() and embedImage() read whatever path you give them. Never pass an unsanitised, user-controlled path, or a request could read arbitrary files off your server.

docs.title: Automatic inline images
docs.text:
You don't have to call embedImage() yourself for every image. By default the renderer scans the HTML body for <img> sources, turns the embeddable ones into inline parts, and rewrites the reference to a cid: URL — so the images travel with the message instead of being hot-linked. Two source kinds are embedded:

<?php

$email->html('
    <img src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo...">   <!-- decoded in memory -->
    <img src="/var/www/assets/logo.png">               <!-- read from disk -->
');
  • data: URIs with an image MIME type are decoded and embedded (many clients strip data URIs, so this also improves rendering).
  • Local file paths are embedded when the file exists and is actually an image.
  • http(s):// URLs and existing cid: references are left untouched — remote images are never fetched, and an explicit embedImage() still works exactly as before.

Identical sources are de-duplicated into a single part, and the generated Content-ID is content-derived. Turn the whole pass off per message when you'd rather ship the HTML verbatim:

<?php

$email->autoEmbedImages = false;

Only images are read

Auto-embedding reads a referenced local file only when it sniffs as an image, so an <img src="/etc/passwd"> in HTML is ignored rather than embedded. Even so, treat HTML you put into a message as trusted — don't build it from unsanitised user input.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
The renderer emits the standard envelope and structural headers — From, To, Cc, Reply-To, Subject, Date, Message-ID, MIME-Version, and the content headers — plus everything you added through the Email builder:

<?php

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Receipt')
    ->header('X-Campaign', 'spring-2026')   // arbitrary custom header
    ->returnPath('bounces@example.com')     // -> Return-Path + Sender
    ->priority(1);                          // -> X-Priority: 1 (Highest)
  • Custom headers from ->header() are emitted as-is.
  • ->returnPath() sets both Return-Path and Sender.
  • ->priority() sets X-Priority — but only when it differs from the Normal (3) default, so ordinary mail stays clean.

Structural headers always win

A custom header can't overwrite a structural one. ->header('From', '...') is ignored in favour of the real From. CR and LF are stripped from every header name and value, so untrusted input can't inject extra headers.

render() also records the header set it produced. Call headers() afterward to get it back as an array — used by the message debugger:

<?php

$renderer = new MessageRenderer();
$renderer->render($email);
$headers = $renderer->headers(); // ['From' => '...', 'Subject' => '...', ...]

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
Headers with non-ASCII characters — an accented subject, a display name like Café Owner — are encoded with RFC 2047 "Q" encoding. The address itself stays literal; only the display name is encoded. Pure-ASCII headers are left untouched.

A pure-ASCII display name is wrapped in a quoted-string ("Doe, John" <a@b.com>), with quotes and backslashes escaped, so a comma or other special character can't split one recipient into two.

Both the plain-text and HTML parts are encoded with quoted-printable, with every line ending normalised to CRLF. Quoted-printable soft-wraps long lines at 76 characters, so even a very long unbroken line — or a non-ASCII body — stays within the 998-octet SMTP limit and the whole message is 7-bit clean, without requiring an 8BITMIME-capable server.

docs.title: Word wrap
docs.text:
Quoted-printable soft wrapping is invisible to the reader — it decodes away on delivery. When you want the plain-text part to stay wrapped in the recipient's client, set Email::$wordWrap = true (and $wrapChars, default 76). The renderer then hard-wraps the text at word boundaries before encoding, leaving long space-less tokens such as URLs intact. Word wrap is off by default; the legacy setWordWrap() adapter method drives it.

Current limitations

The renderer is deliberately small for now. Very long non-ASCII header values aren't folded into multiple encoded-words, and non-ASCII attachment filenames are placed in the parameter as-is rather than RFC 2231-encoded (CR/LF and quotes are still stripped/escaped, so they remain safe). This is fine for typical messages.

docs.title: Previewing Mailables
docs.text:
Designing an email is a lot easier when you can see it. Postal can render any Mailable straight to your browser — HTML, plain text, and the raw MIME — without sending a thing.

It's off by default and never runs in production. You opt in per environment.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Two independent locks both have to be open before a preview is reachable:

  1. The environment is not production.
  2. Config\Postal::$enablePreview is true.

Either lock alone keeps previews hidden, so a stray flag can't leak mail in production and a misconfigured environment can't expose it on its own.

Create app/Config/Postal.php (or set the value from .env):

<?php

namespace Config;

use Myth\Postal\Config\Postal as BasePostal;

class Postal extends BasePostal
{
    public bool $enablePreview = true;
}

Or in .env:

postal.enablePreview = true

Never enable this in production

Even with the flag on, Postal refuses to register the preview routes when ENVIRONMENT is production. Leave the flag in your development config and you've got nothing to worry about.

Config\Postal also sets the preview's URI prefix and where it looks for Mailables — see the Config\Postal reference.

Add a pair to $mailableNamespaces for every place your Mailables live:

<?php

public array $mailableNamespaces = [
    'App\Mails'           => APPPATH . 'Mails',
    'Acme\Billing\Mails'  => ROOTPATH . 'modules/Billing/Mails',
];

docs.title: Making a Mailable previewable
docs.text:
The preview needs sample data to render with — a Mailable usually takes a real User, and there isn't one at preview time. Implement Myth\Postal\Previewable and return an instance built from fake data:

<?php

namespace App\Mails;

use Myth\Postal\Mailable;
use Myth\Postal\Previewable;

class WelcomeEmail extends Mailable implements Previewable
{
    public function __construct(private readonly User $user)
    {
        parent::__construct();
    }

    public static function previewInstance(): static
    {
        return new static(User::makeSample());
    }

    protected function build(): void
    {
        // ...
    }
}

Keeping the sample data right here in the class means it travels with the Mailable — discoverable, version-controlled, and refactor-safe. Only Mailables that implement Previewable show up in the preview; the rest are ignored.

Generated Mailables are ready to go

make:mailable scaffolds the implements Previewable clause and a previewInstance() stub for you. Fill in the sample data and you're done.

docs.title: What you'll see
docs.text:
Visit /postal/preview (or whatever you set $previewPath to). The index lists every previewable Mailable with its subject. Click one to open the detail view, which has three tabs:

  • HTML — rendered in a sandboxed <iframe>, so the email's CSS can't bleed into the preview page (or vice versa)
  • Text — your text() body if you supplied one, otherwise the version Postal auto-generates from the HTML
  • Raw MIME — the full message exactly as it goes on the wire, headers and all — handy for debugging encoding or attachments

Attachments are listed by name. Inline cid: images won't render inside the iframe — that's an inherent limit of the sandbox, not a bug in your email.

If a Mailable throws while building its preview, it still appears in the list with an error badge, and its detail page shows the exception inline. One broken Mailable never takes down the whole preview.

docs.title: Building your own preview screen
docs.text:
The preview pages are a thin layer over Myth\Postal\Preview\MailablePreviewer. Use it directly to show previews inside your own admin area. Pass it the namespace → directory pairs to scan; it doesn't read Config\Postal itself:

<?php

use CodeIgniter\Exceptions\PageNotFoundException;
use Myth\Postal\Exceptions\PostalException;
use Myth\Postal\Preview\MailablePreviewer;

$previewer = new MailablePreviewer([
    'App\Mails'          => APPPATH . 'Mails',
    'Modules\Blog\Mails' => ROOTPATH . 'modules/Blog/Mails',
]);

$classes = $previewer->discover(); // sorted Mailable & Previewable class names

try {
    $preview = $previewer->render($class);
} catch (PostalException $e) {
    throw PageNotFoundException::forPageNotFound($e->getMessage());
}

if ($preview->error !== null) {
    echo $preview->error->getMessage();
} else {
    echo $preview->subject;
    echo $preview->htmlBody;    // null when there's no HTML body
    echo $preview->text;        // derived from the HTML when $preview->textAuto is true
    echo $preview->rawMime;
    print_r($preview->attachments); // file names
}
  • discover() returns every class in those directories that extends Mailable and implements Previewable.
  • isPreviewable() is safe to call with untrusted input, such as a URL segment. It checks the class name's shape before the autoloader ever sees it. render() and subject() run the same check themselves.
  • subject($class) builds the Mailable and returns only its subject. It skips the text and MIME rendering, so it's the cheap call for a list screen. Unlike render(), it lets a build error throw, so wrap it in try/catch.
  • render() and subject() throw a PostalException for a class that isn't previewable. Anything thrown while building or rendering the Mailable comes back in $preview->error instead, so one broken Mailable can't take down your page.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Five minutes from composer require to your first email sent and tested.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
composer require myth/postal

CodeIgniter auto-discovers the package — nothing else to register.

docs.title: 2. Configure a mailer
docs.text:
Publish the config file into your application:

php spark publish

Then edit app/Config/Mailer.php:

<?php

namespace Config;

use Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer as PostalMailer;

class Mailer extends PostalMailer
{
    public string $default = 'log'; // switch to 'smtp' for production

    public array $mailers = [
        'log'  => ['transport' => 'log'],
        'smtp' => [
            'transport'  => 'smtp',
            'host'       => 'smtp.example.com',
            'port'       => 587,
            'authType'   => 'login',
            'encryption' => 'tls',
        ],
    ];

    public function __construct()
    {
        parent::__construct();

        // PHP doesn't allow function calls in property defaults, so read secrets here.
        $this->mailers['smtp']['username'] = env('SMTP_USER');
        $this->mailers['smtp']['password'] = env('SMTP_PASS');
    }
}

With default = 'log', every send in development writes the full rendered message to your app log — nothing leaves your machine.

Redeclaring $mailers replaces the package's list rather than adding to it, so list every mailer you want to use.

docs.title: 3. Create a Mailable
docs.text:
Generate a class with Spark:

php spark make:mailable Welcome

That writes app/Mails/Welcome.php. Open it and fill in build():

<?php

namespace App\Mails;

use Myth\Postal\Mailable;

class Welcome extends Mailable
{
    public function __construct(
        private readonly string $name,
        private readonly string $address,
    ) {
        parent::__construct();
    }

    protected function build(): void
    {
        $this->from('hello@example.com', 'Acme')
            ->to($this->address, $this->name)
            ->subject('Welcome aboard')
            ->html("<p>Hi {$this->name}, glad you're here.</p>");
    }
}

docs.title: 4. Send it
docs.text:
<?php

use App\Mails\Welcome;

(new Welcome('Alice', 'alice@example.com'))->send();

Open writable/logs/ and you'll see the subject, headers, and body exactly as they'd go on the wire. When you're ready to deliver for real, set $default = 'smtp' in your config.

docs.title: 5. Test it
docs.text:
<?php

namespace Tests;

use App\Mails\Welcome;
use CodeIgniter\Test\CIUnitTestCase;
use Myth\Postal\Mailer;

final class WelcomeEmailTest extends CIUnitTestCase
{
    public function testWelcomeEmailIsSent(): void
    {
        $fake = Mailer::fake();

        (new Welcome('Alice', 'alice@example.com'))->send();

        $fake->assertSent(Welcome::class);
        $fake->assertSentTo('alice@example.com');
    }
}

Mailer::fake() swaps the transport for an in-memory recorder — nothing leaves your app, and assertSent() verifies the right message went out.

docs.title: Resend
docs.text:
Resend is an email API: you POST a JSON message over HTTPS and it handles delivery. Postal's resend transport talks to that API directly, so all you need is an API key — no SMTP relay, no extra SDK.

Reach for it when Resend is your provider and you'd rather send over its API than its SMTP endpoint: you get the Resend message id back on every send, and Resend's own error messages when a send is rejected. For Amazon's API see the SES mailer; for a plain SMTP server see the SMTP mailer.

docs.title: Configuring a mailer
docs.text:
Create an API key in the Resend dashboard (a "Sending access" key is enough), then add a named mailer that points at the resend transport:

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'resend' => [
        'transport' => 'resend',
    ],
];

public function __construct()
{
    parent::__construct();

    // PHP doesn't allow function calls in property defaults, so read the key here.
    $this->mailers['resend']['key'] = env('RESEND_KEY');
}

Send through it by name, exactly like any other mailer:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com', 'Your Name')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Welcome aboard')
    ->html('<p>Glad to have you with us.</p>');

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('resend')->send($email);

$result->messageId; // the Resend email id on success

The from address must be on a domain you have verified in Resend.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text: Setting Default What it does key (required) Your Resend API key. Resolving the mailer without one throws a PostalException.

docs.title: What gets sent
docs.text:
Postal maps the message onto Resend's API fields:

  • from, to, cc, bcc, reply-to — display names are quoted (or RFC 2047-encoded when non-ASCII).
  • subject, html, text — if you send HTML without a text body, Resend generates the plain-text version itself.
  • Custom headers — anything set with Email::header(), including List-Unsubscribe.
  • Attachments and inline images — sent base64-encoded. Inline images keep their Content-ID, so <img src="cid:logo"> resolves. Images that the renderer auto-embeds (data: URIs and local image paths) are turned into inline attachments the same way.

Resend can't carry two things, so Postal drops them and logs at debug rather than failing the send:

  • a return path (Email::returnPath()) — Resend manages the bounce address itself;
  • a non-default priority (Email::priority()).

docs.title: Tagging messages with metadata
docs.text:
Attach key/value metadata with Email::metadata(). Each pair becomes a Resend tag, which you can filter on in the dashboard and in webhooks:

<?php

$email->metadata('campaign', 'spring_2026')
      ->metadata('tier', 'gold');

Resend restricts tag names and values to ASCII letters, digits, underscores and dashes (A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -), up to 256 characters. A pair that breaks those rules is dropped and logged at debug, so a stray space never bounces a good message. Only the key is logged, never the value.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
A rejected send never throws. When Resend answers with an error status, the transport returns SendResult::fail() carrying Resend's error message, with the decoded response body (including Resend's error name, such as validation_error) as the raw payload. A network failure (DNS, connection refused, timeout) is also returned as a failure, with the exception as the raw payload:

<?php

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('resend')->send($email);

if (! $result->success) {
    log_message('error', 'Resend rejected the message: ' . $result->error);
}

Wrap the mailer in a failover chain to fall back to another provider when Resend is down.

docs.title: DKIM
docs.text: Resend signs your mail with the DKIM keys of your verified domain. It receives JSON rather than raw MIME, so Postal's DKIM decorator can't sign for it — adding a dkim block to a resend mailer throws a configuration error.

docs.title: HTTP clients
docs.text:
The transport sends its request through Myth\Postal\Transport\HttpClientInterface. It takes it from the postalHttpClient service, which by default returns CurlHttpClient: it needs PHP's curl extension and gives up after 10 seconds connecting or 30 seconds in total.

To use an HTTP client your application already has, override that service in app/Config/Services.php and wrap any PSR-18 client (with PSR-17 factories) in Psr18HttpClient. Every API mailer then sends through it:

<?php

namespace Config;

use CodeIgniter\Config\BaseService;
use GuzzleHttp\Client;
use GuzzleHttp\Psr7\HttpFactory;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\HttpClientInterface;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\Psr18HttpClient;

class Services extends BaseService
{
    public static function postalHttpClient(bool $getShared = true): HttpClientInterface
    {
        if ($getShared) {
            return static::getSharedInstance('postalHttpClient');
        }

        $factory = new HttpFactory();

        return new Psr18HttpClient(new Client(), $factory, $factory);
    }
}

docs.title: Testing without calling Resend
docs.text:
The transport also accepts an HttpClientInterface as its second constructor argument (or you can Services::injectMock('postalHttpClient', ...)). Pass your own client that records the request and returns a canned HttpResponse:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Transport\HttpClientInterface;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\HttpResponse;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\ResendTransport;

$http = new class () implements HttpClientInterface {
    public string $body = '';

    public function request(string $method, string $url, array $headers = [], string $body = ''): HttpResponse
    {
        $this->body = $body;

        return new HttpResponse(200, '{"id":"test-id"}');
    }
};

$result = (new ResendTransport(['key' => 're_test'], $http))->send($email);

json_decode($http->body, true); // the JSON Resend would have received

Return a non-2xx response such as new HttpResponse(422, '{"message":"Invalidtofield."}') to exercise the failure path. To assert on mail your application sends, without touching any transport, use Mailer::fake().

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Keys and headers

  • Keep the key out of source control. Read it from the environment (env('RESEND_KEY')), and use a sending-only key so a leaked key can't read or manage your account.
  • No header injection through fields. Addresses, subject and bodies travel as JSON fields, not concatenated header text.
  • Tag values stay out of the log. Dropped metadata is logged by key only.

docs.title: Sendmail & Mail
docs.text:
Not every app talks SMTP directly. When your server already runs a mail transfer agent — Postfix, Exim, or a sendmail shim — the quickest path to the outbox is to hand the message to it and let it do the delivery. Postal offers two transports for exactly that: sendmail pipes the rendered message to a sendmail binary, and mail passes it through PHP's native mail() function.

Both are thin wrappers around the same rendered MIME the smtp transport produces. Reach for them when a local MTA is already configured; reach for the SMTP mailer when you need to authenticate to a remote server, use encryption, or keep a connection alive across a batch.

docs.title: The Sendmail mailer
docs.text:
The sendmail transport opens the configured binary and writes the complete message to it. It invokes the binary with -t, so sendmail reads the recipients straight from the message headers.

Add a named mailer pointing at the sendmail transport and tell it where the binary lives:

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'sendmail' => [
        'transport' => 'sendmail',
        'path'      => '/usr/sbin/sendmail',
    ],
];

Send through it by name, exactly like any other mailer:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com', 'Your Name')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Welcome aboard')
    ->html('<p>Glad to have you with us.</p>');

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('sendmail')->send($email);

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does path /usr/sbin/sendmail Absolute path to the sendmail binary.

That's the only setting. The binary is run as sendmail -oi -t, with -oi so a lone . in the body never ends the message early, and -t so recipients come from the To, Cc, and Bcc headers.

docs.title: The Mail mailer
docs.text:
The mail transport delivers through PHP's built-in mail(). It renders the message, then splits it so the recipients and subject go in as mail()'s own arguments and the remaining headers and body follow — the shape mail() expects.

It takes no settings, so the mailer entry is just the transport name:

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'mail' => ['transport' => 'mail'],
];

<?php

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('mail')->send($email);

Whether mail() itself reaches a real MTA is a matter of your PHP configuration (sendmail_path in php.ini). Postal hands the message off correctly; the rest is up to your server.

Make either one the default

Set public string $default = 'sendmail'; (or 'mail') in your Config\Mailer to route every service('mailer')->send($email) call through it without naming the mailer each time.

docs.title: Blind recipients (Bcc)
docs.text:
Both transports deliver to Bcc recipients. Because they let the MTA fan out the envelope, the blind addresses travel as a Bcc header that the MTA delivers to and then strips before the message goes on the wire — so the recipients each receive their copy without ever seeing one another.

<?php

$email->bcc('audit@example.com');

Nothing extra to configure: add blind recipients to the message and they're handled.

docs.title: The envelope sender
docs.text:
Both transports set the envelope sender (the bounce address) with sendmail's -f flag. The address is your message's return path when you set one, falling back to the From address otherwise:

<?php

$email->from('you@example.com')
    ->returnPath('bounces@example.com'); // -f bounces@example.com

The address is validated and shell-escaped before it reaches the command line, so it can't inject extra arguments. An address that isn't a valid email is dropped rather than passed through, and the MTA falls back to its own default sender.

docs.title: Testing without the system
docs.text:
Neither transport touches the real popen/mail() machinery directly — each talks through a small seam, so the delivery logic is fully unit-testable.

  • Sendmail writes through Myth\Postal\Transport\SendmailProcess. The shipped PopenProcess opens the real binary; pass your own implementation as the transport's second argument to capture what would have been written.
  • Mail calls through Myth\Postal\Transport\MailFunction. The shipped NativeMailFunction invokes mail(); pass your own to assert on the arguments.
<?php

use Myth\Postal\Transport\MailTransport;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\SendmailTransport;

$sendmail = new SendmailTransport(['path' => '/usr/sbin/sendmail'], $myFakeProcess);
$mail     = new MailTransport([], $myFakeMail);

Postal's own suite uses doubles for exactly this. They live in the package's tests/ directory — internal test plumbing, not public API, so don't rely on them from your application.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Trust the MTA, not the input

  • Shell injection is blocked. The envelope sender is validated and escaped before it reaches the command line; only the configured binary path (which you control) is used verbatim. Keep path out of user input.
  • Header injection is blocked. CR/LF is stripped from every rendered header and recipient, so an address or subject can't smuggle extra headers. Still, validate addresses at your application boundary.
  • mail() reaches a shell. On most systems PHP's mail() ultimately runs sendmail. The same envelope-sender escaping applies, but treat the whole path as security-sensitive and never feed it unvalidated input.

docs.title: Amazon SES
docs.text:
When you send through Amazon Simple Email Service, you're talking to an HTTP API rather than an SMTP server. Postal's ses transport delivers through the official aws/aws-sdk-php SesV2 client, which signs every request with AWS SigV4 and owns the HTTP connection — so there are no credentials to put on the wire and no signing for you to get right.

Reach for it when you already run on AWS (or want SES's deliverability and tracking) and would rather authenticate with IAM than manage an SMTP password. For a local MTA see the Sendmail & Mail mailers; for a remote SMTP server see the SMTP mailer.

docs.title: Installing the SDK
docs.text:
The AWS SDK is an optional dependency — Postal doesn't pull it into every install. Add it when you want the SES transport:

composer require aws/aws-sdk-php

If the SES transport is used without the SDK present, it throws a Myth\Postal\Exceptions\PostalException telling you to install it.

docs.title: Configuring a mailer
docs.text:
Add a named mailer that points at the ses transport and carries its settings:

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'ses' => [
        'transport' => 'ses',
        'region'    => 'us-east-1',
    ],
];

public function __construct()
{
    parent::__construct();

    // PHP doesn't allow function calls in property defaults, so read secrets here.
    $this->mailers['ses']['key']    = env('SES_KEY');
    $this->mailers['ses']['secret'] = env('SES_SECRET');
}

Send through it by name, exactly like any other mailer:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com', 'Your Name')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Welcome aboard')
    ->html('<p>Glad to have you with us.</p>');

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('ses')->send($email);

$result->messageId; // the SES message id on success

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text: Setting Default What it does region us-east-1 The AWS region your SES account sends from. key (unset) AWS access key id. Omit to use the default credential chain (see below). secret (unset) AWS secret access key. Required when key is set. token (unset) Optional session token for temporary credentials. configurationSet (unset) SES configuration set applied to every send (event publishing, dedicated IPs, etc.). forceRaw false Always send raw MIME instead of letting Postal choose (see below).

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Set key and secret explicitly, or leave them unset to let the AWS SDK resolve credentials from its default provider chain — environment variables, shared credentials files, or the IAM role attached to your EC2/ECS/Lambda runtime. On AWS infrastructure, omitting key/secret and using an IAM role is the recommended setup: there are no long-lived secrets to store or rotate.

<?php

'ses' => [
    'transport' => 'ses',
    'region'    => 'us-east-1',
    // no key/secret — credentials come from the instance role
],

docs.title: Simple vs. raw content
docs.text:
SES accepts two body shapes, and Postal picks the right one for each message:

  • Simple — structured fields (subject, HTML, text) that SES assembles into MIME. Used by default.
  • Raw — the complete MIME message Postal renders itself.

Postal switches to raw automatically when:

  • the message carries attachments or inline images (Simple content can't represent them),
  • the HTML body contains an auto-embeddable image — a data: URI or local image path that the renderer inlines — since the resulting inline part can't ride in Simple content,
  • the message is HTML without an explicit text body — only Postal's renderer generates the plain-text alternative that keeps HTML mail off the bare-HTML spam signal, or
  • you set forceRaw => true (for example, when you sign messages with your own DKIM before handing them to SES).

Everything else — plain text, or HTML with a matching text part — goes as Simple. You don't choose; you just build the message and Postal does the right thing.

docs.title: Tagging messages with metadata
docs.text:
Attach key/value metadata to a message with Email::metadata(). The SES transport maps each pair onto an SES EmailTag, which you can use for filtering CloudWatch metrics and event streams:

<?php

$email->metadata('campaign', 'spring_2026')
      ->metadata('tier', 'gold');

SES restricts tag names and values to ASCII letters, digits, underscores and dashes (A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -), 1–256 characters each. Any pair that breaks those rules is dropped and logged at debug rather than failing the send — so a stray space or colon in a tag never bounces an otherwise-good message. Only the offending key is logged; tag values are never written to the log.

Metadata is ignored by transports that have no tagging concept (SMTP, sendmail, mail, log).

docs.title: Configuration sets
docs.text:
Point the mailer at an SES configuration set to apply it to every message — useful for event publishing (deliveries, bounces, complaints), dedicated IP pools, or custom tracking:

<?php

'ses' => [
    'transport'        => 'ses',
    'region'           => 'us-east-1',
    'configurationSet' => 'transactional',
],

docs.title: Testing without calling AWS
docs.text:
The transport takes a SesV2Client as its second constructor argument, so you can unit-test against a mocked client with no network access. Build a client with the AWS SDK's MockHandler:

<?php

use Aws\MockHandler;
use Aws\Result;
use Aws\SesV2\SesV2Client;
use Myth\Postal\Transport\SesTransport;

$mock = new MockHandler();
$mock->append(new Result(['MessageId' => 'test-message-id']));

$client = new SesV2Client([
    'region'      => 'us-east-1',
    'version'     => 'latest',
    'credentials' => ['key' => 'test', 'secret' => 'test'],
    'handler'     => $mock,
]);

$transport = new SesTransport([], $client);
$result    = $transport->send($email);

Append a closure instead of a Result to capture the parameters SES would have received, or append an Aws\SesV2\Exception\SesV2Exception to assert the failure path.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
A rejected send never throws. An SES (or AWS) error is caught and returned as SendResult::fail(), carrying the AWS error message and the original exception as its raw payload:

<?php

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('ses')->send($email);

if (! $result->success) {
    log_message('error', 'SES rejected the message: ' . $result->error);
}

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Credentials and headers

  • No secrets on the wire. SigV4 signing means your secret key never leaves the SDK; prefer an IAM role over stored keys wherever you can.
  • Header injection is blocked. Simple content is sent as structured fields (never concatenated into headers), and raw content goes through the same renderer that strips CR/LF from every header. Display names with control characters are encoded, not passed through. Still, validate addresses at your application boundary.
  • Tag values stay out of the log. Dropped metadata is logged by key only, so message metadata can't leak sensitive values into your debug log.

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text: When it's time to send real email, the smtp transport speaks SMTP directly to your mail server. It handles the full conversation — EHLO, authentication, the envelope, and the message body — and supports STARTTLS, implicit SSL/TLS, LOGIN, PLAIN and XOAUTH2 authentication, and connection reuse across a batch.

docs.title: Configuring an SMTP mailer
docs.text:
Transports are wired through configuration, not code. Add a named mailer to your Config\Mailer and point it at the smtp transport, then give it your server's settings:

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'smtp' => [
        'transport'  => 'smtp',
        'host'       => 'smtp.example.com',
        'port'       => 587,
        'authType'   => 'login',
        'encryption' => 'tls',
        'timeout'    => 30,
        'keepAlive'  => false,
    ],
];

public function __construct()
{
    parent::__construct();

    // PHP doesn't allow function calls in property defaults, so read secrets here.
    $this->mailers['smtp']['username'] = env('SMTP_USER');
    $this->mailers['smtp']['password'] = env('SMTP_PASS');
}

Keep credentials out of committed config

Source username and password from your environment with env('SMTP_USER') / env('SMTP_PASS') (backed by .env) in the config's constructor, as shown above — never hardcode them in Config\Mailer, which is committed to version control. Add the variables to .env (which is git-ignored) and to your deployment's secret store.

Send through it by name, exactly like any other mailer:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com', 'Your Name')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Welcome aboard')
    ->html('<p>Glad to have you with us.</p>');

$result = service('mailer')->mailer('smtp')->send($email);

To make SMTP the default for every send, set public string $default = 'smtp'; and call service('mailer')->send($email) with no name.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
Every key in the mailer array beyond transport is an SMTP setting. Anything you omit falls back to a sensible default.

Setting Default What it does host localhost The SMTP server hostname or IP. port 25 The server port. Use 587 for STARTTLS, 465 for implicit SSL. username (none) The auth username. password (none) The auth password, or the OAuth2 access token for xoauth2. authType (none) login, plain, or xoauth2. Leave unset for no authentication. encryption (none) tls for a STARTTLS upgrade, ssl for an implicit TLS connection. timeout 30 Connection timeout in seconds. keepAlive false Reuse one connection across multiple sends. See below. helo (system hostname) The hostname announced in the EHLO command. Defaults to gethostname(). dsn (none) Delivery Status Notification options. See below.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Pick the method your provider expects with authType:

  • login — the classic challenge/response exchange. The most widely supported.
  • plain — username and password sent in a single base64 token.
  • xoauth2 — OAuth2 bearer tokens. Put your access token in password and the account in username.
<?php

'authType' => 'xoauth2',
'username' => 'you@gmail.com',
'password' => $oauthAccessToken,

Leave authType unset for servers that don't require authentication (a local relay, for instance).

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Two encryption modes, matching the two common ports:

STARTTLS (port 587)Implicit SSL (port 465) 

<?php

'port'       => 587,
'encryption' => 'tls',
Connects in the clear, then upgrades the live connection to TLS with STARTTLS.

<?php

'port'       => 465,
'encryption' => 'ssl',
Negotiates TLS immediately, before the SMTP conversation begins.

Port 465 is implicit TLS automatically

Set port => 465 and Postal uses implicit TLS even if you leave encryption unset, per RFC 8314. Setting encryption => 'ssl' is still fine — and is what forces implicit TLS on any other port.

docs.title: Keep-alive
docs.text:
By default each send opens a fresh connection and closes it with QUIT. When you're sending a batch in one request, that handshake-per-message overhead adds up. Set keepAlive to true to reuse a single connection:

<?php

$mailer = service('mailer')->mailer('smtp');

foreach ($users as $user) {
    $mailer->send($welcomeFor($user));
}

The first send connects and authenticates; each later send issues a quick RSET and reuses the open connection. If the server has dropped an idle connection in the meantime, the transport reconnects transparently rather than failing the send.

One connection per mailer instance

Keep-alive lives on the resolved mailer instance, which is cached per name. Grab the mailer once and reuse it for the batch, as shown above.

docs.title: Delivery Status Notifications
docs.text:
SMTP can ask the server to report back on delivery with DSN. Configure it with the dsn key:

<?php

'dsn' => [
    'notify' => 'FAILURE,DELAY',
    'ret'    => 'HDRS',
    'envid'  => 'order-4821',
],
  • notify — when to report: any of SUCCESS, FAILURE, DELAY, or NEVER.
  • ret — how much of the message to return on a bounce: FULL or HDRS (headers only).
  • envid — an envelope identifier echoed back in the notification, handy for correlation.

DSN parameters are only sent when the server advertises DSN support in its EHLO reply. If it doesn't, they're silently skipped — your mail still goes out.

docs.title: When a send fails
docs.text:
Connection and protocol errors don't throw. The transport catches them, drops the connection so the next send starts clean, and returns a failed SendResult with the reason in error:

Could not connect to SMTP server smtp.example.com:587: Connection refused
Lost connection to SMTP server: read timed out
Unexpected reply to "RCPT TO:<bob@example.com>": 550 5.1.1 User unknown

Internally these are Myth\Postal\Exceptions\SmtpException, a subclass of PostalException, but none of them reach your code. ping() reports the same problems by returning false.

docs.title: Testing without a real server
docs.text:
The transport talks through a small seam, Myth\Postal\Transport\SmtpSocket, rather than touching the network directly. The shipped StreamSocket is the real implementation that opens a TCP/TLS stream to your server.

That seam exists so the SMTP conversation is fully testable. Pass your own SmtpSocket as the transport's second argument to drive the protocol in a unit test:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Transport\SmtpTransport;

$transport = new SmtpTransport(['host' => 'mail.test'], $myFakeSocket);

Postal's own suite uses a scripted double for exactly this. That double ships in the package's tests/ directory — it's internal test plumbing, not public API, so don't rely on it from your application.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Handle credentials and untrusted addresses with care

  • Source secrets from the environment. Read username/password from .env via env() in the config's constructor and never commit them in Config\Mailer. See the warning above.
  • SMTP command injection is blocked. CR/LF is stripped from every command line, so an address, HELO name, or DSN value can't smuggle extra SMTP commands. Still, validate addresses at your application boundary.
  • Credentials never reach your logs. A failed AUTH reports against a safe label, so base64-encoded usernames and passwords stay out of exception messages and SendResult errors.
  • Use encryption for authenticated sends. login and plain put your credentials on the wire. Pair them with encryption => 'tls' or 'ssl' so they're never sent in the clear.

docs.title: Suppression & Unsubscribe
docs.text: Two opt-out contracts you can wire into every send: a suppression list that silently removes recipients before the transport runs, and an unsubscribe URL provider that auto-injects the List-Unsubscribe header for single-recipient messages. Both are optional — if you don't bind them, Postal behaves exactly as before.

docs.title: Suppression list
docs.text: A suppression list answers one question: "should this address receive this email right now?" Any address for which the answer is "no" is removed from to, cc, and bcc before the transport is ever called.

docs.title: Implementing the interface
docs.text:
Create a class that implements SuppressionListInterface:

<?php

namespace App\Mail;

use Myth\Postal\Address;
use Myth\Postal\SuppressionListInterface;

class DatabaseSuppressionList implements SuppressionListInterface
{
    public function isSuppressed(Address $recipient): bool
    {
        return db_connect()
            ->table('email_suppressions')
            ->where('email', $recipient->email)
            ->countAllResults() > 0;
    }
}

docs.title: Wiring it up
docs.text:
Point $suppressionList at your class in app/Config/Mailer.php:

<?php

use App\Mail\DatabaseSuppressionList;

public ?string $suppressionList = DatabaseSuppressionList::class;

That's it. MailerManager instantiates the class once per mailer and passes it in automatically.

docs.title: What happens on a send
docs.text:
Postal calls isSuppressed() for every address in to, cc, and bcc. Addresses that return true are dropped silently. If every recipient is suppressed, the transport is never called and send() returns a cancelled result:

<?php

$result = service('mailer')->send($email);

if ($result->cancelled) {
    // all recipients were suppressed — nothing was sent
    // $result->error carries the reason: 'All recipients are suppressed'
}

docs.title: The email.suppressed event
docs.text:
Each removed address fires an email.suppressed event so you can log or audit it:

<?php

use CodeIgniter\Events\Events;
use Myth\Postal\Address;

Events::on('email.suppressed', static function (Address $address): void {
    log_message('info', 'Suppressed send to {email}', ['email' => $address->email]);
});

Register this in your app/Config/Events.php. The event fires before email.sending, so it won't interfere with any cancellation logic you have there.

Suppression runs after email.composing

If a composing listener adds recipients dynamically, those new addresses are also checked against your suppression list. The filter always sees the final recipient set after composing completes.

docs.title: Unsubscribe headers
docs.text: When a subscriber hits "unsubscribe" in their mail client, the client usually follows a List-Unsubscribe header on the message. Postal can inject this header automatically for single-recipient sends.

docs.title: Implementing the interface
docs.text:
Create a class that implements UnsubscribeUrlInterface:

<?php

namespace App\Mail;

use Myth\Postal\Address;
use Myth\Postal\UnsubscribeUrlInterface;

class TokenUnsubscribeUrl implements UnsubscribeUrlInterface
{
    public function urlFor(Address $recipient): string
    {
        $token = hash_hmac('sha256', $recipient->email, env('APP_KEY'));

        return site_url("email/unsubscribe/{$token}");
    }

    public function isOneClick(): bool
    {
        return true; // emit List-Unsubscribe-Post per RFC 8058
    }
}

docs.title: Wiring it up
docs.text:
Point $unsubscribeUrl at your class in app/Config/Mailer.php:

<?php

use App\Mail\TokenUnsubscribeUrl;

public ?string $unsubscribeUrl = TokenUnsubscribeUrl::class;

docs.title: What gets injected
docs.text:
For a message with exactly one To recipient and no existing List-Unsubscribe header, Postal calls urlFor() and writes:

List-Unsubscribe: <https://example.com/email/unsubscribe/abc123>

If isOneClick() returns true, it also adds the RFC 8058 one-click header:

List-Unsubscribe: <https://example.com/email/unsubscribe/abc123>
List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click

The one-click header signals to mail clients (and Gmail in particular) that a POST to your URL is enough to unsubscribe — no confirmation page required.

Multi-recipient messages are skipped

Auto-injection only applies when there's exactly one To recipient. A newsletter blast to 500 addresses doesn't get a header, because one URL can't represent all of them. If you need unsubscribe headers on bulk sends, set them explicitly (see below).

docs.title: Setting the header explicitly
docs.text:
Call listUnsubscribe() on the message to set the header yourself. This always wins over auto-injection:

<?php

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('newsletters@example.com')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Your weekly digest')
    ->html($body)
    ->listUnsubscribe('https://example.com/unsubscribe/weekly?id=42');

This is the right approach for pre-rendered bulk mail where you've already built a per-recipient URL before constructing the message.

Wrapping is handled for you

listUnsubscribe() wraps the URL in angle brackets (<…>) as the RFC requires. Pass the raw URL — don't add the brackets yourself.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Postal ships an in-memory test double so you can assert on what your application would have sent without ever touching a real transport or the network. Call Mailer::fake() at the top of a test; it swaps the bound service('mailer') for a recorder and hands that recorder back to you.

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Mailer;

$fake = Mailer::fake();

// ...exercise the code under test, which sends as usual...
service('mailer')->send($email);

$fake->assertSentTo('user@example.com');

Every mailer resolved from service('mailer') — the default and any named mailer — routes through the same double, so you don't need to know which mailer your code reaches for.

docs.title: Faking sends
docs.text:
Mailer::fake() returns a FakeTransport. From that point on, no message leaves your application: each send is recorded in memory and reports success, so the code under test behaves as though delivery worked.

<?php

$fake = Mailer::fake();

(new WelcomeEmailService())->sendTo($user);

$fake->assertSentCount(1);

Reset between tests

The swap lives in the service container for the rest of the test. If your test case doesn't already reset services, call Services::reset() in tearDown() so one test's fake doesn't leak into the next.

docs.title: Inspecting what was sent
docs.text:
sent() returns the recorded messages as an array of Email objects, in the order they were sent:

<?php

$messages = $fake->sent();

$this->assertSame('Welcome!', $messages[0]->subject);

Pass a content matcher — a closure that receives an Email and returns a bool — to filter:

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$welcomes = $fake->sent(static fn (Email $email): bool => $email->subject === 'Welcome!');

If you send Mailables, pass the class name instead to get just the messages that came from that Mailable:

<?php

$welcomes = $fake->sent(WelcomeEmail::class);

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text: All assertions integrate with PHPUnit, so a failure fails the test with a readable message.

docs.title: assertSent(Closure|string $callback, ?Closure $filter = null)
docs.text:
Passes when at least one recorded message satisfies the matcher. Pass a closure, or a Mailable class name (see below):

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$fake->assertSent(static fn (Email $email): bool =>
    $email->subject === 'Welcome!'
    && str_contains((string) $email->htmlBody, 'Thanks for joining'));

docs.title: By Mailable class
docs.text:
When you send a Mailable, send() tags the message with its class, so you can assert on the type instead of matching content. Pass the class name to assertSent():

<?php

$fake->assertSent(WelcomeEmail::class);

Add a closure as a second argument to narrow it further — both must match:

<?php

$fake->assertSent(
    WelcomeEmail::class,
    static fn (Email $email): bool => $email->subject === 'Welcome aboard',
);

docs.title: assertSentTo(string $email)
docs.text:
Passes when at least one recorded message was addressed to the given email — in any of the To, Cc, or Bcc buckets. The match is case-insensitive:

<?php

$fake->assertSentTo('user@example.com');

docs.title: assertNotSent(Closure $callback)
docs.text:
Passes when no recorded message satisfies the matcher:

<?php

$fake->assertNotSent(static fn (Email $email): bool => $email->subject === 'Password reset');

docs.title: assertNothingSent()
docs.text:
Passes when no message was recorded at all:

<?php

$fake->assertNothingSent();

docs.title: assertSentCount(int $count)
docs.text:
Passes when exactly the given number of messages were recorded:

<?php

$fake->assertSentCount(3);

docs.title: Config\Mailer
docs.text: Config\Mailer defines your named mailers and how sends behave. Publish it with php spark publish to get app/Config/Mailer.php, a Config\Mailer class that extends Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer, and redeclare only the properties you want to change. See Installation.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Property Type Default Description $default string 'null' The mailer used when you don't name one. The null mailer discards every message. $fireEvents bool true Fires the email events, including email.suppressed. false silences all of them. $suppressionList ?class-string null A class implementing SuppressionListInterface. See Suppression list. $unsubscribeUrl ?class-string null A class implementing UnsubscribeUrlInterface. See Unsubscribe headers. $mailers array null and log mailers Named mailers, keyed by name. See Mailer entries. $transports array The built-in transports Transport names mapped to classes. See Transports.

Redeclaring $mailers replaces the list

The property in your class replaces the package's, so list every mailer you use, including null or log if you still want them.

docs.title: Mailer entries
docs.text:
Each entry in $mailers is an array with a transport key, naming an entry in $transports, plus that transport's settings. The whole entry is passed to the transport, and keys it doesn't use are ignored.

<?php

public array $mailers = [
    'smtp' => [
        'transport' => 'smtp',
        'host'      => 'smtp.example.com',
        'port'      => 587,
    ],
];

Naming a mailer that isn't in $mailers, or a transport that isn't in $transports, throws a PostalException when the mailer is first used.

docs.title: null
docs.text: No settings. Discards every message and reports success.

docs.title: log
docs.text:
Key Default Description level 'debug' The PSR-3 log level the message is written at.

See Log.

docs.title: smtp
docs.text:
Key Default Description host 'localhost' Server hostname or IP. port 25 Server port. 465 uses implicit TLS automatically. encryption '' 'tls' for STARTTLS, 'ssl' for implicit TLS. authType none 'login', 'plain' or 'xoauth2'. Without it, Postal doesn't authenticate, even when username and password are set. username none Auth username. password none Auth password, or the OAuth2 access token for xoauth2. timeout 30 Connection timeout in seconds. keepAlive false Reuse one connection across sends. helo gethostname() The hostname sent in EHLO. dsn none ['notify' => …, 'ret' => …, 'envid' => …] delivery status notification options.

See SMTP.

docs.title: sendmail
docs.text: Key Default Description path '/usr/sbin/sendmail' Path to the sendmail binary.

docs.title: mail
docs.text: No settings. Delivers through PHP's mail(). See Sendmail & Mail.

docs.title: ses
docs.text:
Requires composer require aws/aws-sdk-php.

Key Default Description region 'us-east-1' AWS region. key none Access key ID. Leave out with secret to use the AWS default credential chain. secret none Secret access key. Used only when key is set too. token none Session token for temporary credentials. configurationSet none SES configuration set applied to every send. forceRaw false Always send raw MIME.

See Amazon SES.

docs.title: resend
docs.text:
Key Default Description key required Resend API key. Missing or empty throws a PostalException.

See Resend.

docs.title: failover
docs.text:
Key Default Description chain required Mailer names to try, in order. Missing or empty throws a PostalException.

See Failover.

docs.title: dkim
docs.text:
Add a dkim array to an smtp or sendmail mailer to sign its messages. On any other transport it throws a PostalException.

Key Description domain The signing domain. selector The DNS selector for the public key. privateKey A path to a PEM file, or the PEM text.

See DKIM Signing.

docs.title: Secrets and .env
docs.text:
PHP doesn't allow function calls in property defaults, so read secrets in the constructor:

<?php

public function __construct()
{
    parent::__construct();

    $this->mailers['smtp']['username'] = env('SMTP_USER');
    $this->mailers['smtp']['password'] = env('SMTP_PASS');
}

Like any CodeIgniter config, values can also be overridden from .env with the mailer. prefix. For a key inside $mailers, the key must already exist in your config:

mailer.default = smtp
mailer.mailers.smtp.host = smtp.example.com

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
$transports maps a transport name to a class implementing Myth\Postal\Transport\TransportInterface. The defaults are null, log, smtp, sendmail, mail, ses, resend and failover.

To add your own, register the class and point a mailer at it. Postal constructs it with the mailer entry as its only argument:

<?php

public array $transports = [
    // ...the built-in transports...
    'postmark' => \App\Mail\PostmarkTransport::class,
];

public array $mailers = [
    'postmark' => ['transport' => 'postmark', 'token' => ''],
];

Redeclaring $transports replaces the package's map too, so copy the built-in entries from Myth\Postal\Config\Mailer.

A transport implements two methods:

Method Description send(Email $email): SendResult Delivers the message. Return SendResult::fail() when it's rejected; throw only for configuration or connection errors. ping(): bool Returns true when the transport has a usable connection.

docs.title: Config\Postal
docs.text:
Config\Postal holds the settings for features outside the mailer: the browser preview and markdown emails. To change them, create app/Config/Postal.php with a Config\Postal class that extends Myth\Postal\Config\Postal, and redeclare the properties you want to change.

<?php

namespace Config;

use Myth\Postal\Config\Postal as BasePostal;

class Postal extends BasePostal
{
    public bool $enablePreview = true;
}

It is never served when ENVIRONMENT is production, whatever this is set to. $previewPath string 'postal/preview' The URI prefix the preview is served under. $mailableNamespaces array<string, string> ['App\Mails' => APPPATH . 'Mails'] Namespace → directory pairs searched for previewable Mailables.

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
Myth\Postal\Email is the message builder. It is mutable and every builder method returns the same instance, so calls chain. The mailer clones the message when you send it, so changing your Email after send() doesn't affect the message that went out.

<?php

use Myth\Postal\Email;

$email = (new Email())
    ->from('you@example.com', 'Your Name')
    ->to('user@example.com')
    ->subject('Welcome aboard')
    ->html('<p>Glad to have you with us.</p>');

docs.title: Builder methods
docs.text: All builder methods return static.

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
Method Description from(string $address, string $name = '') Sets the sender. replyTo(string $address, string $name = '') Sets the Reply-To address. to(array\|string $address, string $name = '') Adds a recipient. Call it again to add more. cc(array\|string $address, string $name = '') Adds a Cc recipient. bcc(array\|string $address, string $name = '') Adds a Bcc recipient.

to(), cc() and bcc() accept:

  • an address and an optional name: ->to('user@example.com', 'User')
  • a "Name <email>" string: ->to('User <user@example.com>')
  • a list of either form: ->to(['a@example.com', 'B <b@example.com>'])

Every address is validated as it is added. A malformed or empty address throws a Myth\Postal\Exceptions\PostalException from the builder call, not later from the transport.

docs.title: Content
docs.text: Method Description subject(string $subject) Sets the subject line. html(string $html) Sets the HTML body. text(string $text) Sets the plain-text body. When you set HTML without text, the renderer generates the text part — see MIME Rendering.

docs.title: Headers and delivery
docs.text: Method Description header(string $name, string $value) Adds a custom header. Structural headers such as From can't be overridden. priority(int $level) Sets X-Priority, from 1 (highest) to 5 (lowest). 3 is normal and adds no header. returnPath(string $address) Sets the bounce address (Return-Path and Sender). listUnsubscribe(string $url) Sets List-Unsubscribe, wrapping the URL in <…>. Takes precedence over an auto-injected header — see Suppression & Unsubscribe. metadata(string $key, string $value) Adds a provider tag. The SES and Resend transports send these as tags; other transports ignore them.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
Method Description attach(string $path, string $name = '', string $mime = '') Attaches a file by path. The file is read when the message is rendered, not when you call this. attachData(string $data, string $name, string $mime = '') Attaches bytes already in memory. The MIME type defaults to application/octet-stream. embedImage(string $path, string $cid, string $name = '', string $mime = '') Embeds an inline image. Reference it from the HTML as cid:<cid>.

An empty $name falls back to the file's basename, and an empty $mime is detected from the file. See Attachments and inline images.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: The builder methods write to public properties, which you can also read, for example in an event listener.

docs.title: Rendering options
docs.text:
These have no builder method. Set them directly.

Property Type Default Description $autoEmbedImages bool true Embeds data: URIs and local image paths found in the HTML as inline parts. See Automatic inline images. $wordWrap bool false Hard-wraps the plain-text part so the wrapping survives delivery. $wrapChars int 76 The line length $wordWrap wraps at.

docs.text: Property Type Description $mailableClass ?string The class of the Mailable that built the message, or null. Never written into the message. $rawMessage ?string Internal. The signed MIME message that DKIM signing hands to the transport. Don't set it yourself.

docs.title: Address
docs.text:
Myth\Postal\Address is the read-only value object stored in $from, $replyTo, $to, $cc and $bcc.

Member Description $email The address, e.g. user@example.com. $name The display name, or ''. new Address(string $email, string $name = '') Creates an address. Doesn't validate. Address::fromString(string $address) Parses "Name <email>" or a bare address. Doesn't validate. toString() Returns Name <email>, or just the address when there's no name. Address::isValid(string $email) Checks an address. Internationalised domains pass when the intl extension is installed. 
<?php

Events::on('email.sending', static function (Email $message): void {
    foreach ($message->to as $address) {
        log_message('info', 'Sending to {to}', ['to' => $address->toString()]);
    }
});

docs.title: SendResult
docs.text:
Myth\Postal\SendResult is what every send returns: service('mailer')->send(), Mailable::send(), and each transport's send(). It is read-only.

<?php

$result = service('mailer')->send($email);

if (! $result->success) {
    log_message('error', 'Mail failed: ' . $result->error);
}

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Type Description $success bool true when the transport accepted the message. $messageId ?string The message ID, when the transport has one. See the table below. $error ?string Why the send failed or was cancelled. null on success. $raw mixed The provider's response or exception, when there is one. See the table below. $cancelled bool true when the send was stopped before reaching the transport. $success is then false.

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Outcome $success $cancelled $error Sent true false null Failed false false The transport's error message Cancelled by an email.sending listener false true null Cancelled because every recipient was suppressed false true 'All recipients are suppressed'

Check $cancelled before treating a result as a delivery failure: a cancelled send never reached the transport. See Cancelling a send and Suppression list.

When every child of a failover mailer fails, $error lists each child's error: All failover transports failed: …; ….

docs.title: Factories
docs.text:
Transports build results with three static methods. You need them only when writing your own transport or a test double.

Method Result SendResult::ok(?string $messageId = null, mixed $raw = null) A successful send. SendResult::fail(string $error, mixed $raw = null) A failed send. SendResult::cancelled(?string $reason = null) A cancelled send. $reason becomes $error.

A transport should return fail() for a rejected message and throw only for configuration or connection errors.
